ep-abl-001.question: What is the cornerstone of any AF ablation, whatever the energy source used?
commentaires: Incorrect: AV node ablation ("ablate and pace") controls the ventricular rate, not the rhythm; AF persists.
Correct: AF triggers arise mainly in the pulmonary vein sleeves; isolating them is the core step, whatever the energy source.
Incorrect: the cavotricuspid isthmus is the target for typical flutter; a CTI line alone does not treat AF.
Incorrect: the slow pathway is the target for AVNRT and plays no role in maintaining AF.
ep-abl-001.explication: AF triggers (atrial ectopic beats initiating runs of AF) arise predominantly in the muscular sleeves of the pulmonary veins. Electrical pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), whether by radiofrequency, cryoballoon or pulsed field, is therefore the core step, recommended in every AF ablation procedure. CTI ablation treats typical flutter, not AF. AV node ablation is a rate control strategy ("ablate and pace": AV node ablation followed by permanent pacing), not a rhythm control strategy. The slow pathway is the target for AVNRT.
ep-abl-001.aRetenir: AF ablation = pulmonary vein isolation first and foremost.
ep-abl-001.rappel: AF ablation is built on circumferential electrical isolation of the pulmonary veins, performed at the antrum, away from the ostia, so that venous triggers can no longer reach the atrium. Point-by-point radiofrequency, cryoballoon and pulsed field are simply different tools for achieving the same isolation, and the endpoint remains electrophysiological. Additional lesion sets (posterior wall, lines, substrate ablation) have no systematic proven benefit and are reserved for selected cases. Do not confuse with the cavotricuspid isthmus (typical flutter), the slow pathway (AVNRT) or the AV node (a rate-control strategy that requires permanent pacing).

ep-abl-002.question: What is the mechanism of tissue injury in pulsed field ablation (PFA, electroporation)?
options: Resistive heating by alternating current above 50 °C
Intracellular freezing of tissue at around −40 °C
commentaires: Correct: brief high-voltage pulses create irreversible membrane pores and kill the cell with no predominant thermal mechanism.
Incorrect: this is the mechanism of radiofrequency (resistive heating followed by coagulation necrosis), not of pulsed field.
Incorrect: tissue freezing is the mechanism of cryoablation (cryoballoon, cryocatheter).
Incorrect: focused ultrasound has been tried for ablation, but it works by heating and has nothing to do with pulsed field.
ep-abl-002.explication: Pulsed field ablation delivers very brief, high-voltage electrical pulses that create pores in cell membranes; above a certain threshold, electroporation is irreversible and leads to cell death. This mechanism is essentially non-thermal, unlike radiofrequency (resistive heating, coagulation necrosis above about 50 °C) and cryoablation (freezing). Its main advantage is relative tissue selectivity: myocardium is more sensitive than the oesophagus, nerves or vessels. Vigilance is nonetheless required: slight heating can occur with some configurations, and PFA has its own complications (coronary spasm, haemolysis).
ep-abl-002.aRetenir: PFA kills cardiomyocytes by irreversible electroporation, with no predominant thermal mechanism.
ep-abl-002.rappel: The three AF ablation energies work differently. Radiofrequency heats tissue resistively at the catheter contact, with heat then conducted deeper; coagulation necrosis occurs above about 50 °C. Cryoablation kills cells by freezing, with ice crystal formation, and its efficacy depends on the temperature reached and the duration. Pulsed field delivers very brief high-voltage pulses: above a threshold, electroporation becomes irreversible; below it, it is reversible and may cause only transient block. Thresholds differ between tissues, myocardium being the most sensitive, hence a relative rather than absolute tissue selectivity.

ep-abl-003.question: According to the 2024 ESC AF guidelines, where does ablation stand for a 55-year-old patient without structural heart disease who has symptomatic paroxysmal AF and has not yet received any antiarrhythmic drug?
options: Class IIa, only after failure of a first antiarrhythmic drug
Class IIb, reserved for patients with heart failure
Class I, as first-line therapy after shared decision-making
Not recommended: rate control is sufficient at this age
commentaires: Incorrect: prior failure of an antiarrhythmic drug has no longer been a prerequisite in paroxysmal AF since EARLY-AF, STOP AF First and Cryo-FIRST.
Incorrect: heart failure is not a requirement; the indication covers symptomatic paroxysmal AF, including in structurally normal hearts.
Correct: the 2024 ESC guidelines give ablation a class I (level A) recommendation as first-line therapy in paroxysmal AF, after shared decision-making.
Incorrect: in a young symptomatic patient, rhythm control is appropriate and ablation is one of the first-line options.
ep-abl-003.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines give AF ablation a class I (level A) recommendation as a first-line option within a rhythm control strategy in patients with paroxysmal AF, to reduce symptoms, recurrence and progression of AF. This rests notably on the EARLY-AF, STOP AF First and Cryo-FIRST trials, which showed fewer recurrences than with antiarrhythmic drugs. The decision should be shared with the patient, who must be informed of the benefits and risks. Prior failure of an antiarrhythmic drug is therefore no longer a prerequisite in paroxysmal AF, and heart failure is not a requirement; ablation also remains recommended after failure of or intolerance to an antiarrhythmic drug. Settling for rate control in a symptomatic 55-year-old would deprive the patient of a real benefit.
ep-abl-003.aRetenir: ESC 2024: ablation of paroxysmal AF = first-line option (class I), after shared decision-making.
ep-abl-003.rappel: In the 2024 ESC guidelines, ablation is part of a rhythm-control strategy whose primary aim is to improve symptoms and quality of life. It is a class I recommendation in paroxysmal or persistent AF after failure of, or intolerance to, an antiarrhythmic drug and, in paroxysmal AF, as a first-line option. In persistent AF, first-line ablation carries a weaker recommendation and is reserved for selected patients. In HFrEF, it is recommended when arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy is highly likely. In every case the decision is shared, and anticoagulation remains guided by the risk score, regardless of the rhythm strategy.

ep-abl-004.question: During cryoballoon ablation of the right superior pulmonary vein, how is the risk of phrenic nerve palsy classically monitored?
options: Continuous oesophageal temperature monitoring with a probe
Monitoring of impedance and delivered power
Fluoroscopic check of the right hemidiaphragm at the end of the application
Phrenic nerve pacing from the SVC with diaphragmatic monitoring
commentaires: Incorrect: oesophageal temperature monitors the oesophageal risk on the posterior wall, not the phrenic nerve.
Incorrect: impedance and power are radiofrequency parameters; they give no information on phrenic function during a cryoapplication.
Incorrect: checking the hemidiaphragm only at the end of the application is too late; monitoring must be continuous so the application can be stopped at the first sign.
Correct: the right phrenic nerve is paced from the SVC throughout the application while diaphragmatic contraction is monitored (palpation, CMAP).
ep-abl-004.explication: The right phrenic nerve runs along the superior vena cava, close to the right superior pulmonary vein; it is at risk during applications to the right-sided veins, particularly with the cryoballoon. It is paced from the SVC (diagnostic catheter) throughout the application, and diaphragmatic contraction is monitored by abdominal palpation and/or recording of the diaphragmatic compound motor action potential (CMAP), whose fall in amplitude precedes loss of contraction. At the slightest weakening, the application is stopped immediately (rapid termination, or "double stop"), which usually allows recovery. A simple fluoroscopic check at the end of the application would come too late. Oesophageal temperature relates to the oesophageal risk on the posterior wall, and impedance is a radiofrequency parameter.
ep-abl-004.aRetenir: Applications to the right-sided veins = phrenic pacing from the SVC and immediate stop at the slightest diaphragmatic weakening.
ep-abl-004.rappel: The right phrenic nerve runs down along the superior vena cava and then anterior to the right pulmonary veins, especially the superior one; it is therefore at risk during applications on the right-sided veins, particularly with the cryoballoon, and during SVC ablation. Monitoring relies on continuous phrenic pacing upstream of the ablation site, with assessment of diaphragmatic contraction by palpation and/or CMAP recording, whose amplitude falls before contraction is lost. Stopping the application immediately at the first sign of weakening is the only effective way to limit the injury. Most phrenic nerve palsies recover, sometimes over several months.

ep-abl-005.question: True or false: the electrophysiological endpoint of pulmonary vein isolation is entrance block (loss of pulmonary vein potentials) and, ideally, exit block.
commentaires: Correct: isolation is demonstrated by entrance block (PV potentials abolished or dissociated) and ideally exit block, i.e. bidirectional isolation.
Incorrect: the statement is true; a mere reduction in PV potential amplitude is not enough; the expected endpoint is indeed entrance block, supplemented by exit block.
ep-abl-005.explication: Isolation of a pulmonary vein is confirmed by entrance block: the PV potentials recorded by a circular or multipolar catheter disappear or become dissociated from atrial activity. Exit block is confirmed by pacing inside the vein: the venous sleeve is captured locally without conduction to the atrium. Together, these two criteria define bidirectional isolation. A mere reduction in potential amplitude is not enough. A waiting period and/or adenosine testing can help unmask early reconnection.
ep-abl-005.aRetenir: Isolated vein = entrance and exit block, not just reduced potentials.
ep-abl-005.rappel: Entrance block is shown by abolition or dissociation of the venous potentials, and exit block by local capture of the venous sleeve without conduction to the atrium. A classic pitfall is the far-field potential: from the left atrial appendage in the left-sided veins, and from the right atrium or SVC in the right-sided veins. It is distinguished from a true venous potential by pacing manoeuvres (for example pacing from the appendage or the coronary sinus), which advance the far-field electrogram. To detect latent conduction, a waiting period can be observed and an adenosine test performed, which may unmask transient reconnection.

ep-abl-006.question: After AF ablation, how long is the classic "blanking period", during which early recurrences are not counted as failure?
commentaires: Incorrect: one month is too short; lesion inflammation and oedema account for early recurrences well beyond that.
Correct: the expert consensus uses a 3-month blanking period; recurrences during this time do not count as failure.
Incorrect: 6 months exceeds the consensus definition; a recurrence after 3 months already counts as failure.
Incorrect: 12 months is the usual time point for assessing success, not the blanking period.
ep-abl-006.explication: In the weeks after ablation, lesion inflammation and oedema promote early recurrences that do not always predict long-term failure. The expert consensus uses a 3-month blanking period, during which these recurrences are not taken into account when assessing success. After that, recurrence is classically defined as an episode of AF, flutter or atrial tachycardia lasting at least 30 seconds. Very early, repeated recurrences may nevertheless be treated (antiarrhythmic drug, cardioversion) during this period. The pitfall is to conclude too early that the procedure has failed and to schedule a redo within the first month.
ep-abl-006.aRetenir: Blanking = 3 months after AF ablation; thereafter, recurrence = episode ≥ 30 s.
ep-abl-006.rappel: Success after AF ablation is judged using definitions standardised by the expert consensus. Early recurrences, caused by lesion inflammation and oedema, are common and do not mean definitive failure. After the blanking period, any documented AF, atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia lasting at least 30 s counts as a recurrence; success is usually assessed at 12 months. The intensity of monitoring (ECGs, repeated Holter recordings, implantable loop recorder) determines how many recurrences are detected: symptom-driven follow-up underestimates recurrences, particularly asymptomatic ones. Whether to stop anticoagulation is not decided on apparent success alone.

ep-abl-007.question: Regarding pulsed field ablation (PFA) of AF, which statements are correct?
options: It has no tissue selectivity: the oesophageal risk is similar to that of radiofrequency
It can cause coronary spasm, particularly with applications close to a coronary artery (mitral isthmus, cavotricuspid isthmus)
A high number of applications can cause haemolysis, which may affect renal function
It completely removes the need for periprocedural anticoagulation
commentaires: Incorrect: PFA is relatively myocardium-selective; atrio-oesophageal fistula has hardly ever been reported, unlike with radiofrequency.
Correct: coronary spasm has been described with applications close to the arteries (mitral or cavotricuspid isthmus); nitrates are often given.
Correct: intravascular haemolysis is dose-dependent and can cause acute kidney injury; good hydration is advised.
Incorrect: intraprocedural heparin (ACT > 300 s) and uninterrupted oral anticoagulation remain essential, as with thermal energy sources.
ep-abl-007.explication: PFA relatively spares non-myocardial tissue (oesophagus, phrenic nerve, vessels): this is the very opposite of a lack of selectivity, and it explains the near-absence of atrio-oesophageal fistula and persistent phrenic nerve palsy in large series. However, coronary spasm has been described with applications close to the coronary arteries, particularly on the mitral or cavotricuspid isthmus; prophylactic nitrates are often given. Dose-dependent intravascular haemolysis can cause acute kidney injury if the number of applications is high; good hydration is advised. Periprocedural anticoagulation remains essential: heparin during the procedure and uninterrupted oral anticoagulation, as with thermal energy sources.
ep-abl-007.aRetenir: PFA: selective but not risk-free (coronary spasm, haemolysis), and anticoagulation is unchanged.
ep-abl-007.rappel: Each ablation energy has its signature complications. Radiofrequency carries a risk of atrio-oesophageal fistula and pulmonary vein stenosis; the cryoballoon mainly of phrenic nerve palsy, usually reversible; pulsed field of coronary spasm when applications are delivered close to an artery, and of intravascular haemolysis proportional to the number of applications, with a risk of acute kidney injury. Complications common to any left atrial procedure remain whatever the energy: tamponade, stroke or TIA, and vascular access complications. Thromboembolic prevention (uninterrupted DOAC, heparin with an ACT target) is therefore identical for all energies.

ep-abl-008.question: During ablation in the left atrium, what ACT (activated clotting time) target is classically recommended for heparin therapy?
options: No heparin if the patient is on a DOAC
commentaires: Incorrect: an ACT > 150 s is far too low for a left atrial procedure; the thromboembolic risk would be high.
Incorrect: 200 s is still below the consensus target for the left heart.
Correct: the target is an ACT > 300 s from the transseptal puncture onwards (often before), checked every 15 to 30 minutes.
Incorrect: uninterrupted DOAC therapy does not remove the need for intraprocedural heparin; a higher initial dose is often even required.
ep-abl-008.explication: The risk of thromboembolic events during a left atrial procedure calls for unfractionated heparin, started at the latest immediately after transseptal puncture (often before), with a target ACT above 300 seconds, checked regularly (every 15 to 30 minutes). Patients on uninterrupted DOACs often need a higher initial heparin dose to reach this target. Values of 150 or 200 s are insufficient for the left heart. Being on a DOAC does not remove the need for intraprocedural heparin.
ep-abl-008.aRetenir: LA ablation: heparin with ACT > 300 s, even on a DOAC.
ep-abl-008.rappel: Thromboembolic prevention for a left atrial ablation has three parts. Before: uninterrupted oral anticoagulation (DOAC, or VKA with a therapeutic INR), with exclusion of appendage thrombus according to the risk profile. During: unfractionated heparin given before or just after transseptal puncture, titrated to the ACT measured at regular intervals. After: anticoagulation continued for at least 2 months in all patients, whatever the rhythm outcome; beyond that, continuation depends on the thromboembolic risk score (CHA2DS2-VA), not on the apparent success of the ablation.

ep-abl-009.question: A patient has recurrent paroxysmal AF 10 months after a first radiofrequency pulmonary vein isolation. What mechanism is most often found at the redo procedure?
options: Reconnection of one or more pulmonary veins
Atrial macro-reentry around the mitral isthmus
A non-PV trigger located in the superior vena cava
Progression of the left atrial fibrotic substrate
commentaires: Correct: PV reconnection through gaps in the lesion lines is the dominant cause; each vein is checked and re-isolated.
Incorrect: mitral isthmus macro-reentry does occur, mainly after extensive lines, but is much less common than PV reconnection.
Incorrect: non-PV triggers (SVC, coronary sinus) are a possible but minor cause, to be sought after the veins have been checked.
Incorrect: substrate progression matters mainly in persistent AF; in paroxysmal AF, PV reconnection is by far the leading cause.
ep-abl-009.explication: The main cause of AF recurrence after pulmonary vein isolation is electrical reconnection of one or more veins through gaps in the lesion lines. At a redo procedure, the priority is therefore to check the isolation of each vein and re-isolate those that have reconnected. Macro-reentrant atrial tachycardias (mitral isthmus, roof) do occur, mainly after extensive ablation, but are less common than PV reconnection. Non-PV triggers (superior vena cava, coronary sinus, crista terminalis) and progression of the atrial substrate are other mechanisms, minor ones in paroxysmal AF, that are sought once PV isolation has been confirmed.
ep-abl-009.aRetenir: AF recurrence after PVI = first look for and re-isolate reconnected veins.
ep-abl-009.rappel: The durability of isolation depends on lesion quality and continuity: with radiofrequency, contact force, power, duration, catheter stability and spacing between points; with cryoablation, complete occlusion of the vein and the quality of the application. Any gap in the line allows reconnection, the dominant cause of recurrence after PVI. At a redo procedure, isolation of each vein is checked first and any reconnected vein is re-isolated. If all veins have remained isolated, other mechanisms are sought: non-PV foci (SVC, coronary sinus, crista terminalis, left atrial appendage), macro-re-entrant atrial tachycardias or atrial substrate.

ep-abl-010.question: What was the main (intention-to-treat) result of the CABANA trial comparing ablation with drug therapy in AF?
options: A significant reduction in all-cause mortality with ablation
A significant reduction in disabling stroke with ablation
No significant difference in the primary composite endpoint
Superiority of drug therapy for quality of life
commentaires: Incorrect: all-cause mortality was not significantly reduced in the intention-to-treat analysis; this is the classic trap.
Incorrect: disabling stroke was part of the composite endpoint and was not significantly reduced on its own.
Correct: in the ITT analysis, the composite of death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding or cardiac arrest was not significantly reduced (8.0% vs 9.2%).
Incorrect: quite the opposite; ablation improved quality of life and reduced AF recurrence.
ep-abl-010.explication: CABANA randomised 2204 patients with AF to ablation or drug therapy (rhythm or rate control). In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary composite endpoint (death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, cardiac arrest) was not significantly reduced (8.0% vs 9.2%, HR 0.86), and none of its components, mortality or stroke, was reduced on its own. Interpretation is complicated by substantial crossover (more than a quarter of the drug arm underwent ablation) and a lower than expected event rate. The per-protocol and as-treated analyses suggest a benefit, and ablation reduced AF recurrence and improved quality of life. The trap is to claim that CABANA demonstrated a mortality benefit.
ep-abl-010.aRetenir: CABANA: no significant benefit on the hard endpoint in ITT, but fewer recurrences and better quality of life.
ep-abl-010.rappel: A randomised trial is interpreted first by intention to treat: each patient is analysed in the arm to which they were randomised, which preserves comparability between groups. Per-protocol and as-treated analyses lose the benefit of randomisation and only generate hypotheses. A high crossover rate between arms and a lower than expected event rate dilute the difference and reduce power, which can make a trial neutral without ruling out an effect. In practice, AF ablation is indicated to improve symptoms and quality of life; a mortality benefit has not been demonstrated in the general AF population.

ep-abl-011.question: Which population was enrolled in the CASTLE-AF trial?
options: AF with preserved LVEF, no implanted device
AF with LVEF ≤ 35%, with an ICD or CRT-D
Permanent AF with narrow QRS, candidates for ablate and pace
Paroxysmal AF under 65 years, no heart disease
commentaires: Incorrect: CASTLE-AF targeted heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; preserved LVEF was not studied.
Correct: patients with AF, NYHA II–IV, LVEF ≤ 35%, with an ICD or CRT-D, which made it possible to measure AF burden.
Incorrect: permanent AF with narrow QRS treated with AV junction ablation and CRT corresponds to APAF-CRT.
Incorrect: young patients with structurally normal hearts and paroxysmal AF were studied in trials such as EARLY-AF, not CASTLE-AF.
ep-abl-011.explication: CASTLE-AF enrolled patients with paroxysmal or persistent AF, NYHA class II to IV heart failure, LVEF ≤ 35% and an ICD or CRT-D (which allowed AF burden to be tracked precisely). Ablation reduced the primary endpoint of death or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure (28.5% vs 44.6%, HR 0.62), as well as all-cause mortality. This trial underpins the 2024 ESC AF guideline recommendation to consider ablation in selected patients with AF and HFrEF (class I if arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy is highly likely). The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines are more cautious: they consider the trials inconclusive for hard endpoints and give ablation only a class IIa (level C) recommendation, requiring a high AF burden, continuous persistent AF of less than one year's duration and a clear causal link between AF and HF. Permanent AF with narrow QRS corresponds to APAF-CRT, and young patients with structurally normal hearts and paroxysmal AF to trials such as EARLY-AF.
ep-abl-011.aRetenir: CASTLE-AF: AF + HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 35%) with ICD/CRT-D; ablation reduces death and HF hospitalisation.
ep-abl-011.rappel: In heart failure, AF can be either the cause or the consequence of LV dysfunction. Arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy refers to dysfunction caused by the arrhythmia that regresses, at least partly, once sinus rhythm is restored or the rate is controlled. Implanted devices (ICD, CRT-D) allow objective measurement of AF burden, a more reliable endpoint than symptoms for judging the effect of ablation. AF ablation trials in HF differ in their populations (HFrEF with a device, end-stage HF, comparison with rate control), which limits extrapolation. The best candidate is the patient in whom a causal link between AF and HF is likely.

ep-abl-012.question: What is the main message of the EAST-AFNET 4 trial?
options: First-line ablation reduces mortality compared with antiarrhythmic drugs
Early rhythm control allows anticoagulation to be stopped
Rhythm control increases stroke in elderly patients
Early rhythm control reduces cardiovascular events
commentaires: Incorrect: the trial did not compare ablation with antiarrhythmic drugs; rhythm control relied mainly on antiarrhythmic drugs.
Incorrect: anticoagulation was continued according to thromboembolic risk, regardless of the rhythm achieved.
Incorrect: no excess of stroke was observed; stroke was part of the composite endpoint that was reduced.
Correct: rhythm control started within one year of diagnosis reduced the composite of CV death, stroke, HF hospitalisation or ACS (HR 0.79).
ep-abl-012.explication: EAST-AFNET 4 randomised 2789 patients with AF diagnosed less than one year earlier and cardiovascular comorbidities to early rhythm control or usual care (rhythm control reserved for symptoms). Early rhythm control reduced the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, stroke, hospitalisation for heart failure or acute coronary syndrome (HR 0.79), with no excess in the safety endpoint. Rhythm control relied mainly on antiarrhythmic drugs; only a minority of patients underwent ablation (about one fifth at 2 years). Anticoagulation was continued according to thromboembolic risk, regardless of rhythm.
ep-abl-012.aRetenir: EAST-AFNET 4: early rhythm control (< 1 year) = fewer CV events, with anticoagulation maintained.
ep-abl-012.rappel: AF is a progressive disease: repeated episodes promote electrical and structural atrial remodelling, which makes the arrhythmia more likely to persist. Early rhythm control means acting soon after diagnosis, before this remodelling is established, with antiarrhythmic drugs and/or ablation. The 2024 ESC guidelines suggest considering early rhythm control in selected patients, beyond the goal of symptom relief. Whatever rhythm is achieved, anticoagulation remains guided by the thromboembolic risk score, because AF may recur without symptoms; rhythm control and stroke prevention are two independent decisions.

ep-abl-013.question: True or false: the ADVENT trial showed that pulsed field ablation was superior in efficacy to thermal ablation (radiofrequency or cryoballoon) in paroxysmal AF.
commentaires: Incorrect: ADVENT was a non-inferiority trial; it did not show superior efficacy (73.3% vs 71.3% at one year).
Correct: PFA proved non-inferior, not superior, to thermal ablation for both efficacy and safety.
ep-abl-013.explication: ADVENT randomised 607 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal AF to pulsed field ablation or thermal ablation (radiofrequency or cryoballoon). The trial was designed for non-inferiority and met its endpoints: one-year efficacy of 73.3% for PFA vs 71.3% for thermal ablation, and comparable safety (serious adverse events 2.1% vs 1.5%). It therefore did not show superior efficacy. PFA stands out mainly for shorter procedures and a different complication profile. Over-interpreting a non-inferiority result is a classic trap.
ep-abl-013.aRetenir: ADVENT: PFA non-inferior (not superior) to thermal ablation for efficacy and safety.
ep-abl-013.rappel: A non-inferiority trial aims to show that a new treatment is not worse than the reference treatment by more than a prespecified margin. If it meets its objective, the conclusion is non-inferiority, not superiority: superiority can only be claimed if a superiority test was planned in the protocol and is significant. This design is justified when the new treatment offers other advantages (speed, complication profile, simplicity). For PFA, these practical advantages and its distinct safety profile, rather than a gain in efficacy, explain its rapid uptake.

ep-abl-014.question: In the APAF-CRT trial (mortality arm), which strategy was compared with pharmacological rate control in patients with symptomatic permanent AF, narrow QRS and at least one heart failure hospitalisation?
options: AV junction ablation combined with CRT
AV junction ablation and VVI pacing from an apical RV lead
commentaires: Correct: AV junction ablation + CRT versus pharmacological rate control, with a reduction in all-cause mortality (HR 0.26).
Incorrect: pure apical RV pacing induces dyssynchrony; APAF-CRT chose CRT precisely to avoid this.
Incorrect: appendage occlusion prevents stroke but does not control rate; it was not evaluated here.
Incorrect: APAF-CRT dealt with permanent AF, in which pulmonary vein isolation was not the strategy evaluated.
ep-abl-014.explication: APAF-CRT compared AV junction ablation combined with CRT with optimal rate-control drug therapy in patients with permanent AF, narrow QRS (≤ 110 ms) and at least one heart failure hospitalisation, regardless of LVEF. The mortality arm (133 patients) showed a reduction in all-cause mortality (11% vs 29%, HR 0.26), following a first arm showing a reduction in the composite of death, hospitalisation and worsening HF. CRT was chosen to avoid the dyssynchrony induced by pure right ventricular pacing. These results underpinned the 2024 ESC AF guideline recommendation to consider "ablate and pace" with CRT in this population. They also underpin a new recommendation in the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines (class IIa, level B1): highly symptomatic permanent AF, poorly controlled rate despite treatment, and at least one HF hospitalisation. Appendage occlusion and pulmonary vein isolation do not address this question of rate control in permanent AF.
ep-abl-014.aRetenir: APAF-CRT: AV junction ablation + CRT reduces mortality in permanent AF with narrow QRS and HF hospitalisation (ESC 2026 HF: IIa).
ep-abl-014.rappel: Ablate and pace combines AV junction ablation with permanent ventricular pacing: the ventricular rate is fully controlled and regular, but AF persists. The patient becomes irreversibly pacemaker-dependent, and anticoagulation remains guided by the thromboembolic risk score. Exclusive right ventricular pacing may cause dyssynchrony and LV dysfunction, so physiological pacing is preferred, CRT or conduction system pacing depending on the available evidence. This strategy is aimed at patients with permanent AF who remain highly symptomatic or in heart failure despite optimal rate-control medication.

ep-abl-015.question: Which trial evaluated AF ablation in patients with end-stage heart failure being assessed for transplantation or a left ventricular assist device?
commentaires: Incorrect: CASTLE-AF enrolled patients with HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 35%) and an ICD, but not with end-stage heart failure.
Incorrect: EAST-AFNET 4 evaluated early rhythm control in recently diagnosed AF, not end-stage heart failure.
Correct: CASTLE-HTx enrolled patients with end-stage HF referred to a transplant centre; it was stopped early for benefit.
Incorrect: RAFT-AF compared ablation with rate control in AF with HF, without targeting patients awaiting transplantation or a device.
ep-abl-015.explication: CASTLE-HTx randomised 194 patients with end-stage heart failure and symptomatic AF, referred to a transplant centre, to ablation (plus medical therapy) or medical therapy alone. Ablation reduced the composite endpoint of death, left ventricular assist device implantation or urgent transplantation (8% vs 30%, HR 0.24), to the extent that the trial was stopped early for benefit. Its predecessor, CASTLE-AF, dealt with less advanced HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 35%, ICD recipients); RAFT-AF compared ablation with rate control in AF with heart failure; and EAST-AFNET 4 studied early rhythm control in recently diagnosed AF. CASTLE-HTx nevertheless remains a small, open-label trial that was stopped early. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines consider the randomised trials inconclusive for hospitalisation and mortality: they give ablation only a class IIa (level C) recommendation, in carefully selected patients with a high AF burden, continuous persistent AF of less than one year's duration and a clear causal link between AF and HF.
ep-abl-015.aRetenir: CASTLE-HTx: ablation benefits even end-stage HF, but the 2026 ESC HF guidelines reserve ablation for highly selected HFrEF patients (IIa C).
ep-abl-015.rappel: Critical appraisal of a trial must take its design into account. A small, open-label trial stopped early for benefit tends to overestimate the size of the effect, and a composite endpoint that includes events decided by the care team (urgent transplantation, LVAD implantation) is more vulnerable to the lack of blinding. Guidelines weigh these limitations and grade the level of evidence accordingly. For AF ablation in heart failure, the key selection criterion remains a probable causal link between the arrhythmia and LV dysfunction, which should be established before offering the procedure.

ep-abl-016.question: True or false: in the EARLY-AF and STOP AF First trials, first-line cryoablation reduced atrial arrhythmia recurrence compared with antiarrhythmic drug therapy in patients with paroxysmal AF.
commentaires: Correct: in both trials, first-line cryoablation significantly reduced atrial arrhythmia recurrence at one year.
Incorrect: the statement is true; EARLY-AF and STOP AF First were positive for recurrence; they were simply not designed to assess mortality or stroke.
ep-abl-016.explication: EARLY-AF (303 patients, continuous monitoring with an implantable monitor) and STOP AF First (203 patients) compared cryoballoon ablation with first-line antiarrhythmic drugs in patients who had not yet received rhythm-control antiarrhythmic therapy. In both trials, cryoablation significantly reduced atrial arrhythmia recurrence at one year, with a low rate of serious complications. These data, together with Cryo-FIRST, led the 2024 ESC guidelines to recommend ablation as a first-line option in paroxysmal AF. These trials were not designed to assess mortality or stroke.
ep-abl-016.aRetenir: EARLY-AF and STOP AF First: first-line cryoablation reduces recurrence compared with antiarrhythmic drugs.
ep-abl-016.rappel: First-line ablation trials compared ablation with antiarrhythmic drugs in patients with paroxysmal AF who had not yet received rhythm-control therapy. Their primary endpoint is recurrence of atrial arrhythmia (AF, atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia) after the blanking period, and detection depends on monitoring: an implantable loop recorder detects far more episodes than intermittent Holter recordings. The results (EARLY-AF, STOP AF First, Cryo-FIRST) are consistent and underpin the 2024 ESC class I recommendation for first-line ablation in paroxysmal AF, with shared decision-making. None of these trials was powered for mortality or stroke.

ep-abl-017.question: What was the main result of the FIRE AND ICE trial?
options: Non-inferiority of the cryoballoon for efficacy and safety
Superiority of radiofrequency for recurrence at one year
Superiority of the cryoballoon in long-standing persistent AF
An excess of tamponade in the cryoballoon group
commentaires: Correct: in paroxysmal AF, the cryoballoon was non-inferior to radiofrequency for efficacy (failure 34.6% vs 35.9%) and safety.
Incorrect: no superiority of radiofrequency was shown; failure rates were virtually identical.
Incorrect: FIRE AND ICE enrolled only patients with paroxysmal AF; persistent AF was not studied.
Incorrect: overall safety was comparable; the complication more common with the cryoballoon was phrenic nerve palsy, not tamponade.
ep-abl-017.explication: FIRE AND ICE randomised 762 patients with symptomatic drug-refractory paroxysmal AF to PVI with the cryoballoon or with radiofrequency. The cryoballoon proved non-inferior for efficacy (clinical failure endpoint at about 1.5 years of follow-up: 34.6% vs 35.9%) and for overall safety, with no superiority of either technique. The complication profiles differ: phrenic nerve palsy was more common with the cryoballoon (mostly reversible), procedure time was shorter, and there was no excess of tamponade. The trial did not address persistent AF.
ep-abl-017.aRetenir: FIRE AND ICE: cryoballoon non-inferior to radiofrequency for PVI in paroxysmal AF.
ep-abl-017.rappel: The cryoballoon isolates each pulmonary vein in a single-shot application: the balloon is positioned at the ostium, occlusion is confirmed by contrast injection, and the tissue in contact is then frozen. Point-by-point radiofrequency, guided by electroanatomical mapping, creates a continuous line of lesions and is more versatile for lesions outside the veins. For PVI in paroxysmal AF, both techniques have broadly equivalent efficacy and safety. The choice depends on operator experience, venous anatomy and complication profile: phrenic nerve palsy is more frequent with the cryoballoon, while the risk of tamponade does not differ.

ep-abl-018.question: What is the target for ablation of typical atrial flutter?
commentaires: Incorrect: a mitral isthmus line treats some atypical perimitral left atrial flutters, not typical flutter.
Correct: the typical flutter circuit necessarily passes through the cavotricuspid isthmus; a blocked line interrupts it.
Incorrect: a roof line targets left atrial macro-reentry (often after AF ablation), not right-sided typical flutter.
Incorrect: pulmonary vein isolation is the core step of AF ablation.
ep-abl-018.explication: Typical flutter is a right atrial macro-reentry circulating around the tricuspid annulus and necessarily passing through the cavotricuspid isthmus (between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid annulus). A radiofrequency (or other energy) line across this isthmus interrupts the circuit, with a success rate above 90%. The pulmonary veins concern AF; the mitral isthmus and the left atrial roof are line targets for some atypical left atrial flutters, often after AF ablation.
ep-abl-018.rappel: Typical atrial flutter is isthmus-dependent: in its common form it rotates counterclockwise around the tricuspid annulus (viewed en face), with negative sawtooth flutter waves in the inferior leads and positive waves in V1; the less common clockwise form uses the same circuit in the opposite direction. The cavotricuspid isthmus, between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid annulus, is the most accessible and narrowest part of the circuit. Atypical flutters, not isthmus-dependent, revolve around other obstacles (mitral annulus, left atrial roof, surgical or ablation scars), and their ablation requires mapping.

ep-abl-019.question: This tracing was recorded in a patient who has already been cardioverted twice for the same arrhythmia. What is the most appropriate rhythm management?
commentaires: Incorrect: the slow pathway is the target for AVNRT; saw-tooth atrial activity is not due to AV nodal reentry.
Incorrect: pulmonary vein isolation treats AF; it does not interrupt right-sided typical flutter.
Correct: recurrent symptomatic typical flutter: CTI ablation is class I, more effective than antiarrhythmic drugs and low-risk.
Incorrect: long-term amiodarone is less effective than ablation and carries substantial toxicity; it is not first choice.
ep-abl-019.explication: The tracing shows flutter with 2:1 conduction (saw-tooth atrial activity at around 300/min, ventricular rate around 150/min). For recurrent symptomatic typical flutter, cavotricuspid isthmus ablation has a class I recommendation from the ESC, as it is more effective than antiarrhythmic drugs and carries a low risk. The thromboembolic risk of flutter is considered comparable to that of AF: anticoagulation is decided according to the risk score and is required around the procedure. Slow pathway ablation treats AVNRT, pulmonary vein isolation treats AF, and long-term amiodarone is less effective and more toxic than ablation in this indication.
ep-abl-019.aRetenir: Recurrent symptomatic typical flutter: cavotricuspid isthmus ablation first line.
ep-abl-019.rappel: In typical flutter, the atrial rate is around 250–350/min; 2:1 conduction produces a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at about 150 bpm, and flutter should always be considered at that rate. Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs, by slowing the flutter, can allow 1:1 conduction with a very fast ventricular rate, so they must be combined with an AV nodal blocking agent. Thromboembolic risk is managed as for AF, including around cardioversion or ablation. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation, highly effective and low-risk, is the reference strategy for recurrent typical flutter.

ep-abl-020.question: What is the expected procedural endpoint after cavotricuspid isthmus ablation?
options: Termination of flutter during the radiofrequency application
A 50% fall in the amplitude of the isthmus electrograms
Non-inducibility of flutter with rapid atrial pacing
Bidirectional isthmus block demonstrated by pacing
commentaires: Incorrect: termination during the application does not prove that the line is complete; recurrence is then common.
Incorrect: reduced amplitude indicates a lesion, but is no proof of block.
Incorrect: non-inducibility is an inadequate endpoint, abandoned because it poorly predicts recurrence.
Correct: the validated endpoint is bidirectional block, confirmed by pacing on either side of the line (coronary sinus and low lateral wall).
ep-abl-020.explication: Termination of flutter during the application does not prove that the line is complete: recurrence is then common, and non-inducibility of flutter is also an inadequate endpoint. The validated endpoint is bidirectional isthmus block: when pacing from the coronary sinus (septal side), activation must travel around the atrium via the septum and roof to reach the low lateral wall from top to bottom, and vice versa when pacing from the low lateral wall. Widely split double potentials along the line and differential pacing also help. Reduced electrogram amplitude indicates a lesion, but is no proof of block.
ep-abl-020.aRetenir: Typical flutter: success is judged by bidirectional isthmus block, not by termination of the tachycardia.
ep-abl-020.rappel: Several tools confirm isthmus block. The activation sequence during pacing on either side of the line shows whether the wavefront travels around the atrium instead of crossing the isthmus. Along the line, complete block produces widely separated double potentials with an isoelectric interval; a fractionated electrogram within that interval suggests a gap. Differential pacing consists of pacing first close to, then further from, the line: with block, moving away from the line shortens the time to the other side, because the wavefront takes the detour route; with persistent slow conduction, this time lengthens.

ep-abl-021.question: After a cavotricuspid isthmus line, pacing is performed from the coronary sinus ostium. Which activation pattern of the right atrial lateral wall indicates isthmus block in the septal-to-lateral direction?
options: Collision of the two wavefronts in the mid lateral wall
Caudocranial, with the low lateral region activated first
Craniocaudal, with the low lateral region activated last
Simultaneous activation along the whole lateral wall
commentaires: Incorrect: collision on the lateral wall means that one wavefront still crosses the isthmus; isthmus conduction persists.
Incorrect: caudocranial activation shows that the wavefront is crossing the isthmus, hence no block.
Correct: with the isthmus blocked, the wavefront ascends the septum, crosses the roof and descends the lateral wall; the low lateral region is activated last.
Incorrect: simultaneous activation is incompatible with a single wavefront travelling around the atrium; it suggests an annotation error.
ep-abl-021.explication: Before ablation, pacing from the coronary sinus ostium produces two wavefronts: one crosses the isthmus and activates the low lateral wall early (caudocranial activation), the other ascends the septum; the two wavefronts meet on the lateral wall. When block is complete in the septal-to-lateral direction, the wavefront can no longer cross the isthmus: it ascends the septum, crosses the roof and descends the lateral wall, which is then activated craniocaudally, the low region just lateral to the line being activated last. Caudocranial activation, or collision of the wavefronts on the lateral wall, indicates persistent (possibly slowed) isthmus conduction. Block in the other direction is then checked by pacing from the low lateral wall, and differential pacing can be added.
ep-abl-021.aRetenir: Isthmus block: when pacing from the CS ostium, the lateral wall is activated craniocaudally, the low lateral region last.
ep-abl-021.rappel: Isthmus block must be checked in both directions. When pacing from the low lateral wall, lateral-to-septal block forces the wavefront to ascend the lateral wall, cross the roof and descend the septum, so the coronary sinus ostium is activated late, after the high septal region. Without block, the wavefront crosses the isthmus and activates the CS ostium early. A pitfall is very slow conduction across the isthmus, which can mimic block on the activation sequence alone; double potentials along the line and differential pacing make the distinction. Unidirectional block is not enough.

ep-abl-022.question: True or false: after successful cavotricuspid isthmus ablation for typical flutter, the risk of subsequently developing AF is low and does not warrant any specific follow-up.
commentaires: Incorrect: typical flutter and AF share the same substrate; AF develops in more than a third of patients in the medium term after CTI ablation.
Correct: AF is common after CTI ablation; rhythm monitoring and anticoagulation according to the risk score remain appropriate.
ep-abl-022.explication: Typical flutter and AF share the same atrial substrate and often coexist. After successful isthmus ablation, a large proportion of patients (often estimated at more than a third, or even half in the medium term depending on the series) develop AF. Rhythm monitoring must therefore be maintained, and anticoagulation should not be stopped solely because the ablation was successful: the decision is based on the thromboembolic risk score. This is a common pitfall in clinic.
ep-abl-022.aRetenir: AF often develops after flutter ablation: monitor and anticoagulate according to the risk score.
ep-abl-022.rappel: Typical flutter and AF are two expressions of the same atrial disease: AF may precede flutter, follow it or coexist with it, and flutter often arises from an episode of AF that becomes organised. In a patient treated for AF with a class IC drug or amiodarone, typical flutter may emerge on treatment; isthmus ablation then allows the drug to be continued (hybrid strategy). Isthmus ablation eliminates the flutter circuit, not the AF substrate. Thromboembolic risk is assessed as in AF, using the CHA2DS2-VA score, and does not disappear after ablation.

ep-abl-023.question: In ablation of typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT), where is the targeted slow pathway classically located?
options: Apex of Koch's triangle, near the His recording
Base of Koch's triangle, near the coronary sinus ostium
Right ventricular outflow tract, below the pulmonary valve
Posteroseptal mitral annulus, via a transseptal approach
commentaires: Incorrect: the apex of the triangle houses the compact node and the His bundle; ablating there risks complete AV block.
Correct: the slow pathway lies in the inferior and posterior part of Koch's triangle, between the coronary sinus ostium and the tricuspid annulus.
Incorrect: the RV outflow tract is the site of idiopathic PVCs and VT, unrelated to the nodal slow pathway.
Incorrect: a left-sided approach is reserved for rare leftward extensions of the slow pathway, after failure of the standard right-sided approach.
ep-abl-023.explication: The slow pathway lies in the inferior and posterior part of Koch's triangle, between the coronary sinus ostium and the tricuspid annulus. Ablation is performed there, away from the compact AV node and the His bundle, which lie at the apex of the triangle near the tendon of Todaro. Ablating close to the His bundle risks complete AV block. An approach to the posteroseptal mitral region is considered only for rare leftward extensions of the slow pathway, after failure of the right-sided approach. The RV outflow tract is a site of idiopathic PVCs/VT.
ep-abl-023.aRetenir: Slow pathway = inferior part of Koch's triangle, away from the His bundle.
ep-abl-023.rappel: Koch's triangle is bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the insertion of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and, at its base, the coronary sinus ostium. The compact AV node and the His bundle lie at its apex; the fast pathway approaches the node superiorly, near the His, and the slow pathway through the inferoposterior region, near the CS ostium. Slow pathway ablation therefore starts low in the triangle and moves up only cautiously, as the risk of AV block rises towards the apex. Cryoablation, whose effect is reversible during cryomapping, is an alternative close to the node, at the cost of a higher recurrence rate.

ep-abl-024.question: During a radiofrequency application to the slow pathway, an accelerated junctional rhythm with 1:1 retrograde conduction to the atria is observed. What does it mean?
options: Fast pathway injury requiring the application to be stopped
Imminent complete AV block, requiring the procedure to stop
Catheter too far from the slow pathway, to be repositioned
A probably effective site, with VA conduction monitored
commentaires: Incorrect: as long as VA conduction remains 1:1, the fast pathway is preserved; it is loss of VA conduction that requires stopping.
Incorrect: this rhythm does not in itself herald AV block; it becomes worrying if it is very fast or if VA conduction is lost.
Incorrect: quite the opposite; junctional rhythm is a sensitive marker of an application at an effective site.
Correct: a sensitive (though non-specific) marker of an effective site; retrograde VA conduction is monitored continuously throughout the application.
ep-abl-024.explication: Junctional rhythm during the application is a sensitive (but non-specific) marker of an effective slow pathway ablation site: it does not indicate that the site is too far away. Retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction must be monitored continuously: as long as it remains 1:1, the fast pathway is preserved. Loss of retrograde conduction (VA block), a very fast junctional rhythm or PR prolongation should prompt immediate termination of the application, as they herald injury to the fast pathway or the compact node. It is therefore not in itself a sign of imminent AV block or of fast pathway injury.
ep-abl-024.aRetenir: Junctional rhythm during slow pathway ablation = effective site; stop immediately if VA conduction is lost.
ep-abl-024.rappel: Slow pathway ablation is highly effective in typical AVNRT, with a low but real risk of AV block. During the application, the warning signs that require immediate cessation are loss of retrograde VA conduction during junctional rhythm, a very fast junctional rhythm, and PR prolongation or AV block. The procedural endpoint is non-inducibility of the tachycardia, including on isoprenaline: elimination of slow pathway conduction is not required, and a persistent AH jump with at most a single nodal echo is accepted. Junctional rhythm points to a good site but is not in itself a criterion of success.

ep-abl-025.question: Regarding AVNRT ablation, which statements are correct?
options: The risk of AV block requiring a pacemaker is around 5%
Cryoablation increases the risk of AV block but reduces recurrence
It is contraindicated in young patients
commentaires: Correct: slow pathway ablation cures more than 95% of AVNRT, hence its status as the treatment of choice.
Incorrect: in experienced centres, the risk of AV block requiring a pacemaker is below 1%.
Incorrect: quite the opposite; cryoablation reduces the risk of AV block at the cost of a slightly higher recurrence rate.
Incorrect: young age is rather an argument for ablation, which avoids long-term drug therapy.
ep-abl-025.explication: Slow pathway ablation is the treatment of choice for recurrent symptomatic AVNRT (class I in the 2019 ESC guidelines), with a success rate above 95% and a risk of AV block requiring pacing below 1% (not around 5%). Cryoablation allows reversible testing (cryomapping) and reduces the risk of AV block, which makes it attractive in children or when the anatomy is high-risk, at the cost of a slightly higher recurrence rate: it therefore does not reduce recurrence. Young age is not a contraindication: it is often an argument for ablation, which avoids long-term drug therapy.
ep-abl-025.aRetenir: AVNRT: slow pathway ablation, > 95% success, AV block < 1%; cryoablation reduces the risk of AV block but has a slightly higher recurrence rate.
ep-abl-025.rappel: Typical (slow–fast) AVNRT conducts down the slow pathway and back up the fast pathway: atrial activation is almost simultaneous with the QRS, with a very short RP interval (pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-S in the inferior leads). Atypical forms (fast–slow, slow–slow) have a longer RP interval. All forms use the slow pathway, whose ablation therefore treats every variant. Acutely, vagal manoeuvres then adenosine; in the long term, ablation is recommended first-line in symptomatic patients with recurrences. The choice between radiofrequency and cryoablation depends on anatomy and AV block risk: safety takes priority over lower recurrence rates.

ep-abl-026.question: During an EP study, how is dual AV nodal physiology demonstrated with atrial extrastimulus testing?
ep-abl-026.reponseAttendue: By an AH "jump" of ≥ 50 ms for a 10 ms decrement in the coupling interval of the atrial extrastimulus (A1A2): conduction suddenly switches from the fast pathway (blocked, longer refractory period) to the slow pathway. This jump is often accompanied by an echo beat or by induction of AVNRT.
ep-abl-026.explication: Normally, the AH interval lengthens progressively as the extrastimulus coupling interval is shortened. With dual AV nodal physiology, the fast pathway has a longer refractory period than the slow pathway: when the extrastimulus falls within the refractory period of the fast pathway, conduction switches abruptly to the slow pathway, with an AH jump of at least 50 ms for a 10 ms reduction in coupling interval. This jump may be followed by an atrial echo or by induction of the tachycardia. Dual AV nodal physiology is also found in people without AVNRT; it is therefore not sufficient for the diagnosis without an inducible, consistent tachycardia. Conversely, its absence does not rule out AVNRT.
ep-abl-026.aRetenir: Dual AV nodal physiology = AH jump ≥ 50 ms for a 10 ms shortening of the A1A2 coupling interval.
ep-abl-026.rappel: The AV node conducts decrementally: the earlier the extrastimulus, the longer the AH interval, in a continuous fashion when there is no dual physiology. With dual AV nodal physiology, a fast pathway (rapid conduction, long refractory period) and a slow pathway (slow conduction, short refractory period) coexist; block in the fast pathway switches conduction to the slow pathway, hence the discontinuous curve. If the delay in the slow pathway allows the fast pathway to recover, the impulse returns up it: an atrial echo, then sustained AVNRT. Retrograde dual physiology is sought with ventricular extrastimuli (HA jump), and isoprenaline often helps induction.

ep-abl-027.question: What are the two classic approaches for ablation of a left lateral accessory pathway?
options: Retrograde aortic or subxiphoid epicardial approach
Internal jugular or left subclavian approach
commentaires: Incorrect: the retrograde aortic approach is standard, but the subxiphoid epicardial approach is not a standard route to left lateral pathways.
Incorrect: the transseptal approach is standard, but the coronary sinus serves as a landmark; only some epicardial or posteroseptal pathways are ablated there.
Correct: the mitral annulus is reached transseptally (atrial aspect) or via the retrograde aortic route (ventricular aspect), depending on anatomy and operator preference.
Incorrect: superior venous routes do not provide practical access to the mitral annulus for ablation.
ep-abl-027.explication: Left-sided accessory pathways insert on the mitral annulus. They are reached either via the transseptal approach (puncture of the interatrial septum and atrial approach to the annulus) or via the retrograde aortic approach (femoral arterial access, crossing the aortic valve and approaching the ventricular aspect of the annulus). The choice depends on operator preference and anatomy. The coronary sinus serves mainly as a landmark and for recording along the mitral annulus; some epicardial or posteroseptal pathways may require ablation within the coronary sinus or its branches, but this is not the standard approach to left lateral pathways.
ep-abl-027.aRetenir: Left-sided accessory pathway: transseptal or retrograde aortic approach.
ep-abl-027.rappel: An accessory pathway is first localised on the pre-excited ECG (polarity of the delta wave and QRS), then by mapping the annulus. The coronary sinus catheter, running along the mitral annulus, brackets a left-sided pathway. During pre-excitation, the target is the earliest ventricular activation, preceding the delta wave; during orthodromic AVRT or ventricular pacing, the earliest retrograde atrial activation; an accessory pathway potential is a good marker of a successful site. Left lateral pathways are the most common. The retroaortic approach has its own complications (aortic valve, coronary arteries), and the transseptal approach those of septal puncture.

ep-abl-028.question: This is the baseline sinus rhythm ECG of a patient who presents to the emergency department in pre-excited AF and is haemodynamically stable. Which treatments must be avoided?
commentaires: Correct, to be avoided: by slowing the AV node, calcium channel blockers promote conduction over the accessory pathway, with a risk of VF.
Correct, to be avoided: digoxin slows the AV node and shortens the accessory pathway refractory period; risk of acceleration and VF.
Incorrect, may be used: these antiarrhythmic drugs slow conduction over the accessory pathway and may be given to a stable patient.
Incorrect, may be used: electrical cardioversion is the treatment of choice if the patient is unstable and remains safe in a stable patient.
ep-abl-028.explication: The baseline tracing shows pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave). In pre-excited AF, AV nodal blocking drugs (rate-slowing calcium channel blockers, digoxin, IV beta-blockers, adenosine) must be avoided, as must IV amiodarone (class III in the 2019 ESC guidelines): by blocking the AV node, they may promote conduction over the accessory pathway, accelerate the ventricular response and precipitate VF. Electrical cardioversion, by contrast, is the treatment of choice if the patient is unstable and remains a safe option in a stable patient; IV ibutilide or procainamide, which slow conduction in the accessory pathway, may also be used depending on availability. Subsequently, accessory pathway ablation is recommended in these high-risk patients.
ep-abl-028.aRetenir: Pre-excited AF: never an AV nodal blocking drug; electrical cardioversion, then accessory pathway ablation.
ep-abl-028.rappel: In pre-excited AF, impulses reach the ventricles via the accessory pathway without the decremental filter of the AV node: a fast, irregular, broad-QRS tachycardia with varying morphology. The risk of VF depends on pathway properties: a shortest pre-excited RR interval during AF (SPERRI) ≤ 250 ms, a short antegrade refractory period, multiple pathways or inducible AVRT are high-risk markers. Intermittent pre-excitation, or abrupt loss of pre-excitation on exercise, suggests a low-risk pathway. In asymptomatic patients, risk stratification (EP study) guides ablation; after an episode of pre-excited AF, ablation is recommended.

ep-abl-029.question: True or false: ablation of an anteroseptal or para-Hisian accessory pathway carries a higher risk of AV block than ablation of a left lateral pathway, which may favour cryoablation.
commentaires: Correct: these pathways lie next to the His bundle and compact node; cryoablation, with its reversible testing (cryomapping), limits the risk of AV block.
Incorrect: the statement is true; a left lateral pathway is far from the conduction system, whereas a para-Hisian pathway carries a genuine risk of AV block.
ep-abl-029.explication: Anteroseptal and para-Hisian accessory pathways lie immediately adjacent to the His bundle and the compact AV node. Radiofrequency ablation there carries a real risk of AV block, unlike left lateral pathways, which are far from the conduction system. Cryoablation, thanks to reversible cryomapping and catheter adherence, allows the site to be tested and this risk to be limited, at the cost of a slightly higher recurrence rate. Precise mapping, including a His recording, is essential before any application.
ep-abl-029.aRetenir: Para-Hisian or anteroseptal pathway: risk of AV block, consider cryoablation.
ep-abl-029.rappel: Septal accessory pathways are divided into anteroseptal or para-Hisian, midseptal and posteroseptal (inferoparaseptal) pathways. The closer the pathway is to the upper Koch's triangle, the higher the risk of injuring the compact node or the His bundle: recording a His potential at the ablation site is a warning sign. For these pathways, careful mapping and cautious applications with monitoring of AV conduction are preferred, or cryoablation with reversible cryomapping. Posteroseptal pathways, usually far from the His, may instead be epicardial and require an approach via the coronary sinus or its branches.

ep-abl-030.question: What was the main result of the VANISH trial?
options: Ablation reduced death, storm or appropriate shocks
Ablation reduced all-cause mortality by almost half
Ablation made it possible to defer ICD implantation
commentaires: Correct: ablation reduced the composite of death, electrical storm or appropriate shock (HR 0.72) compared with escalation of antiarrhythmic drugs.
Incorrect: mortality alone did not differ significantly between the two arms.
Incorrect: quite the opposite; escalation of antiarrhythmic drugs (amiodarone, mexiletine) did worse than ablation.
Incorrect: all patients already had an ICD; ablation complements the ICD, it does not replace it.
ep-abl-030.explication: VANISH randomised 259 patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and an ICD who had VT despite antiarrhythmic drug therapy to ablation or escalation of antiarrhythmic drugs (increased amiodarone or addition of mexiletine). Ablation reduced the composite endpoint of death, electrical storm or appropriate shock (HR 0.72). Mortality alone did not differ significantly. All patients kept their ICD: ablation does not remove the need for one. These data underpin the 2022 ESC recommendation to favour ablation over antiarrhythmic drug escalation in this situation.
ep-abl-030.aRetenir: VANISH: in ischaemic VT on antiarrhythmic drugs, ablation is better than escalating the drugs.
ep-abl-030.rappel: Monomorphic VT after myocardial infarction is due to re-entry around and through the scar, within bundles of surviving myocardium with slow conduction. The ICD treats it (ATP, shock) but does not prevent it; repeated shocks impair quality of life and are associated with a worse prognosis. Two options reduce recurrences: antiarrhythmic drugs (amiodarone, possibly combined with mexiletine, at the cost of significant long-term side effects) or ablation, which targets the substrate directly. Ablation reduces recurrences and ICD therapies; it does not replace the ICD and has not been shown to reduce mortality alone.

ep-abl-031.question: On a bipolar voltage map of the left ventricle, which cut-offs are classically used to define dense scar and border zone?
options: Dense < 0.1 mV; border 0.1–0.5 mV; healthy > 0.5 mV
Dense < 0.5 mV; border 0.5–1.5 mV; healthy > 1.5 mV
Dense < 0.5 mV; border 0.5–8.3 mV; healthy > 8.3 mV
Dense < 1.5 mV; border 1.5–5 mV; healthy > 5 mV
commentaires: Incorrect: these cut-offs are too low; myocardium at 0.5 mV bipolar is already abnormal.
Correct: Marchlinski's bipolar cut-offs, the most widely used: dense scar < 0.5 mV, border zone 0.5–1.5 mV, healthy myocardium > 1.5 mV.
Incorrect: 8.3 mV is the LV unipolar voltage cut-off, useful for intramural or epicardial substrate, not the bipolar cut-off.
Incorrect: these cut-offs are too high; a bipolar voltage of 2 to 5 mV corresponds to healthy myocardium.
ep-abl-031.explication: The bipolar cut-offs validated by Marchlinski and widely used in practice are: normal myocardium > 1.5 mV, border zone between 0.5 and 1.5 mV, dense scar < 0.5 mV. VT isthmuses often lie within channels of relatively preserved voltage inside the scar, which is why the colour thresholds are adjusted to reveal them. These values depend on electrode size, interelectrode spacing and wavefront direction: they must be interpreted together with the electrograms. The cut-off of about 8.3 mV applies to LV unipolar voltage, used to detect intramural or epicardial substrate: it must not be confused with the bipolar cut-offs.
ep-abl-031.aRetenir: LV bipolar voltage: < 0.5 mV dense scar, 0.5–1.5 mV border zone, > 1.5 mV normal.
ep-abl-031.rappel: Bipolar voltage, measured between two closely spaced electrodes, mainly reflects local subendocardial tissue; unipolar voltage, measured against a distant reference, has a wider field of view and can reveal intramural or epicardial substrate beneath endocardium that looks normal on bipolar mapping. Amplitude depends on contact, electrode size and spacing, and the direction of the activation wavefront: the same tissue may look more or less abnormal depending on the catheter or the mapping rhythm. A voltage map delineates the substrate but does not show which channels take part in the VT: it is complemented by electrogram analysis and pacing manoeuvres.

ep-abl-032.question: What are late potentials and LAVA in VT substrate ablation, and why is it worth eliminating them?
ep-abl-032.reponseAttendue: They are abnormal, fractionated, low-voltage electrograms recorded within scar: late potentials occur after the end of the QRS, while LAVA (local abnormal ventricular activities) are abnormal local signals distinct from the far-field signal, occurring during or after the QRS. They reflect slow conduction through bundles of surviving myocardium that may be involved in VT circuits. Their elimination is a substrate ablation endpoint, usable even when VT is not tolerated or not inducible, and it is associated with fewer recurrences.
ep-abl-032.explication: Ablation guided by activation and entrainment mapping requires an inducible, well-tolerated VT, which is often not the case. Substrate ablation is performed in sinus or paced rhythm, targeting areas of slow conduction. Late potentials are isolated electrograms after the end of the surface QRS; LAVA more broadly are fractionated, high-frequency signals that may be hidden within the QRS and unmasked by pacing or manoeuvres. Their complete elimination was associated with better recurrence-free survival in the study by Jaïs et al. Other substrate strategies exist (scar homogenisation, scar dechanneling, mapping of deceleration zones).
ep-abl-032.aRetenir: Late potentials and LAVA = markers of slow conduction within scar; their elimination is a substrate ablation endpoint.
ep-abl-032.rappel: A scar-related VT circuit comprises an isthmus of surviving myocardium, bounded by non-excitable tissue, where conduction is slow, and an exit site into healthy myocardium. Substrate ablation targets these areas without the need to induce or tolerate the VT. Besides analysis of abnormal electrograms, pace mapping helps to locate the circuit: pacing at the exit site reproduces the QRS of the clinical VT, and a long stimulus-to-QRS delay indicates pacing within an area of slow conduction. Markers of effective substrate ablation are elimination of the targeted abnormal signals and non-inducibility at the end of the procedure.

ep-abl-033.question: During a haemodynamically tolerated post-infarction VT, entrainment from a site within the scar shows concealed fusion, a post-pacing interval (PPI) equal to the VT cycle length (TCL) (difference < 30 ms) and a stimulus-to-QRS interval equal to the electrogram-to-QRS interval, representing 45% of the cycle length. Where is the catheter?
commentaires: Incorrect: at the exit site, the S-QRS/cycle length ratio is below 30%; here it is 45%.
Incorrect: an outer loop gives manifest fusion during entrainment, not concealed fusion.
Incorrect: a bystander gives a PPI clearly longer than the cycle length and an S-QRS longer than the EGM-QRS.
Correct: concealed fusion, PPI − TCL ≤ 30 ms, S-QRS = EGM-QRS and an S-QRS/TCL ratio of 30 to 50% define the central isthmus.
ep-abl-033.explication: According to Stevenson's criteria, concealed fusion (paced QRS identical to the VT QRS) indicates that the site is protected, within or close to the scar. A PPI close to the cycle length (PPI − TCL ≤ 30 ms) indicates that the site is part of the circuit, which excludes a bystander, where the PPI is prolonged. A stimulus-to-QRS interval equal to the electrogram-to-QRS interval confirms that the site is in the circuit, and an S-QRS/TCL ratio of roughly 30 to 50% defines the central isthmus (below 30%: exit; 50 to 70%: proximal isthmus; above 70%: inner loop). An outer loop would give manifest fusion. This is an ideal ablation site, where VT usually terminates quickly.
ep-abl-033.aRetenir: Concealed fusion + PPI − TCL ≤ 30 ms + S-QRS = EGM-QRS at 30–50% of the cycle length = central isthmus.
ep-abl-033.rappel: Entrainment means pacing slightly faster than the tachycardia (typically 10–30 ms below its cycle length): each stimulus enters the circuit and resets it, and the VT resumes at its own cycle length when pacing stops. It proves a re-entrant mechanism. Manifest fusion indicates pacing outside the protected isthmus; concealed fusion, pacing within or adjacent to a protected zone. The PPI is measured on the local electrogram at the pacing site: the further the site from the circuit, the more the PPI exceeds the cycle length. Pitfalls: lack of true capture, termination or change of the VT, and decremental conduction falsely prolonging the PPI.

ep-abl-034.question: A 35-year-old woman with a structurally normal heart has highly symptomatic monomorphic PVCs with LBBB morphology and inferior axis (probable RVOT origin). According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, where does ablation stand?
options: Ablation after failure of two antiarrhythmic drugs
Primary prevention ICD followed by surveillance
commentaires: Correct: the 2022 ESC guidelines recommend first-line ablation for symptomatic PVCs/VT from the RV outflow tract.
Incorrect: no prior drug failure is required; beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers are merely alternatives.
Incorrect: with no structural heart disease or arrhythmic risk factor, there is no indication for an ICD.
Incorrect: in a young woman with a normal heart, the toxicity of long-term amiodarone is not justified.
ep-abl-034.explication: PVCs from the right ventricular outflow tract (LBBB morphology with inferior axis) are the most common idiopathic ventricular arrhythmias. The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend first-line ablation for symptomatic PVCs/VT from the RVOT, given its high success rate and low risk. Beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are alternatives. Amiodarone is not a first-line treatment in a young patient with a normal heart. There is no indication for an ICD in the absence of structural heart disease or arrhythmic risk.
ep-abl-034.rappel: Idiopathic ventricular arrhythmias occur in a structurally normal heart, which must be confirmed (ECG, echocardiography, sometimes MRI). Their morphology points to the site: LBBB pattern with inferior axis and late precordial transition for the RV outflow tract; earlier transition for the LV outflow tract or aortic cusps; RBBB pattern with left axis for fascicular VT, which is verapamil-sensitive. The mechanism is often focal (triggered activity) and the prognosis is good. Treatment is guided by symptoms and the impact on LVEF: beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker or ablation depending on the site, which determines efficacy and risk.
ep-abl-034.legende: Monomorphic PVCs with LBBB morphology and inferior axis on the 12-lead ECG

ep-abl-035.question: Regarding PVC-induced cardiomyopathy, which statements are correct?
options: The risk increases with PVC burden (typically above 10 to 20% of beats)
PVC ablation can lead to recovery of LVEF
It is seen only with PVCs of epicardial origin
commentaires: Correct: the risk becomes notable above a burden of about 10% and substantial above 20%.
Correct: suppressing the PVCs often allows LVEF to recover, which retrospectively confirms the diagnosis.
Incorrect: the origin of the PVCs matters little; outflow tract PVCs, the most common, are a classic cause. It is the burden that counts.
Incorrect: on the contrary, the dysfunction is often reversible once the PVCs are suppressed.
ep-abl-035.explication: A high PVC burden (in practice above about 10%, the risk becoming substantial above 20%) can cause left ventricular dysfunction, which is reversible once the PVCs are suppressed. In unexplained LV systolic dysfunction with a high PVC burden, this diagnosis should be considered and ablation (or drug therapy) offered; the 2022 ESC guidelines recommend ablation in this situation. The main determinant is the burden, not the site of origin: outflow tract PVCs, which are endocardial, are a common cause. Recovery of LVEF after ablation retrospectively confirms the diagnosis. Claiming irreversibility is therefore wrong; the difficulty lies in distinguishing PVC-induced cardiomyopathy from a primary cardiomyopathy with PVCs.
ep-abl-035.aRetenir: High PVC burden + reduced LVEF: think PVC-induced cardiomyopathy, potentially reversible after ablation.
ep-abl-035.rappel: PVC burden is quantified on Holter monitoring (percentage of beats); it varies from day to day, so prolonged or repeated recordings are useful. Besides burden, other factors are associated with the risk of dysfunction: wide-QRS PVCs, interpolated PVCs and duration of exposure. Before concluding that cardiomyopathy is PVC-induced, underlying heart disease must be sought (cardiac MRI is useful), because PVCs may be the consequence rather than the cause. The diagnosis is confirmed in retrospect by improvement in LVEF after suppression of the PVCs. Ablation or drug therapy are the options, the choice depending on the site and the patient's profile.

ep-abl-036.question: True or false: according to the 2022 ESC guidelines, in a patient with ischaemic heart disease and recurrent symptomatic sustained monomorphic VT despite amiodarone, ablation is recommended in preference to escalation of antiarrhythmic drug therapy.
commentaires: Correct: the 2022 ESC guidelines recommend (class I) ablation rather than antiarrhythmic drug escalation in this situation, based on VANISH.
Incorrect: the statement is true; drug escalation did worse than ablation in VANISH; ablation is what is recommended.
ep-abl-036.explication: The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend (class I) ablation rather than escalation of antiarrhythmic drugs in patients with ischaemic heart disease and recurrent symptomatic sustained monomorphic VT, or ICD shocks for VT, despite amiodarone therapy. This recommendation is based mainly on the VANISH trial. It does not remove the need for an ICD if one is indicated. Ablation may also be considered earlier, from the first episode, in selected patients.
ep-abl-036.aRetenir: Recurrent ischaemic VT on amiodarone: ablation rather than antiarrhythmic drug escalation.
ep-abl-036.rappel: The 2022 ESC guidelines give ablation a major role in monomorphic VT in ischaemic heart disease. It is recommended for incessant VT or electrical storm refractory to antiarrhythmic drugs, and for recurrent symptomatic VT or shocks despite amiodarone. It may be considered earlier, after the first episode, in selected patients with an ICD. Ablation is ideally discussed in an experienced centre, with prior assessment of the scar (imaging) and of the haemodynamic risk of the procedure. The indication for an ICD, based on the risk of sudden cardiac death, remains independent of that for ablation.

ep-abl-037.question: On a 3D activation (LAT) map of a focal atrial tachycardia, using the standard colour scale, where is the site of origin?
commentaires: Incorrect: grey usually represents scar (very low voltage) or an unmapped area.
Incorrect: purple denotes the latest activation.
Correct: by convention, red denotes the earliest activation, from which activation spreads centrifugally in a focal tachycardia.
Incorrect: blue corresponds to late activation, just before purple.
ep-abl-037.explication: By convention, electroanatomical mapping systems code local activation times (LAT) from red (earliest) to purple (latest), through orange, yellow, green and blue. In a focal tachycardia, activation spreads centrifugally from a red area: this is the ablation target. Grey is usually used to represent scar (very low voltage) or unmapped areas. The operator can change the scale, so the legend should always be checked.
ep-abl-037.aRetenir: Activation map: red = early, purple = late.
ep-abl-037.rappel: An activation map measures, at each point, the local activation time (LAT) relative to a stable reference, often a coronary sinus electrogram. The window of interest is set to the tachycardia cycle length; its position determines how colours are assigned, especially in re-entry. Annotation is made at the onset of the bipolar electrogram or at the maximum negative slope of the unipolar electrogram. In a focal tachycardia, the site of origin precedes the onset of the surface P wave, and the unipolar electrogram shows a QS pattern there. A map is only reliable if point density is sufficient, particularly around the earliest area.

ep-abl-038.question: What is the main principle underlying ablation catheter localisation in the CARTO system?
options: Voltage gradients between skin patches alone
A weak magnetic field detected by a tip sensor
Biplane fluoroscopy combined with image registration
Intracardiac echo tracking the catheter in real time
commentaires: Incorrect: localisation by voltage gradients (impedance) alone is the original principle of EnSite NavX; CARTO uses it as an adjunct.
Correct: coils under the table emit an ultra-low magnetic field, detected by a sensor in the catheter tip.
Incorrect: fluoroscopy remains useful but is not the localisation principle; 3D mapping is used precisely to reduce it.
Incorrect: intracardiac echocardiography can be integrated into the map, but it does not localise the catheter.
ep-abl-038.explication: The CARTO system relies on an ultra-low magnetic field generated by coils placed under the table (location pad).
