A magnetic sensor built into the catheter tip allows its position and orientation to be calculated with high precision. Recent versions add impedance-based localisation to display other catheters that lack a magnetic sensor; impedance-only localisation is the original principle of the EnSite NavX system. Fluoroscopy remains useful, but its use is greatly reduced thanks to these systems. Intracardiac echocardiography can be integrated, but it is not the localisation principle.
ep-abl-038.aRetenir: CARTO = magnetic localisation (sensor in the catheter), supplemented by impedance.
ep-abl-038.rappel: Electroanatomical mapping links each catheter position to electrical information (activation time, voltage) to reconstruct the anatomy in 3D. Magnetic localisation calculates the sensor position from the field emitted by several reference coils: it is accurate and stable but requires catheters fitted with a sensor. Impedance-based localisation, more universal, is used to display the other electrodes. These systems allow lesions to be tagged, the map to be merged with CT, MRI or intracardiac echocardiography, and fluoroscopy to be greatly reduced. Their accuracy may be degraded by patient movement, respiration or displacement of the reference.

ep-abl-039.question: True or false: the EnSite system (formerly NavX) is historically based on a magnetic field emitted by coils under the table, so that only catheters fitted with a dedicated sensor can be displayed.
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is wrong; this is the principle of CARTO; EnSite NavX originally localised electrodes using voltage gradients between skin patches.
Correct: EnSite is historically based on impedance (skin patches), which localises any electrode, and has only recently incorporated magnetic technology.
ep-abl-039.explication: The statement actually describes the CARTO system. The EnSite NavX system uses three pairs of orthogonal skin patches that pass a low-amplitude, high-frequency current; the voltage measured at each electrode is used to calculate its position (impedance-based localisation). Advantage: any electrode on any catheter can be displayed, with no dedicated sensor. Drawback: the field is not homogeneous (variations in tissue impedance), hence correction by modelling. Subsequent generations (EnSite Precision, EnSite X) added magnetic sensors to combine both technologies. The Rhythmia system also uses a hybrid magnetic and impedance approach.
ep-abl-039.aRetenir: EnSite = originally impedance-based localisation, now hybrid with magnetic.
ep-abl-039.rappel: With impedance-based localisation, skin patches create electrical fields across the thorax, and the voltage picked up by each electrode reflects its position, so any catheter can be displayed. The relationship between voltage and distance is not linear, however, because tissue impedance (lungs, blood, fat) varies; the system applies a correction (field scaling). Impedance changes during the procedure (saline infusion, respiration, fluid loading) can distort or shift the geometry. Hybrid systems combine the accuracy of magnetic tracking with the universality of impedance.

ep-abl-040.question: On a complete activation map of an atrial tachycardia, activation times span more than 90% of the cycle length and the earliest area lies next to the latest ("early meets late"). What mechanism does this suggest?
commentaires: Incorrect: decremental conduction is a nodal property, unrelated to the distribution of atrial activation times.
Incorrect: micro-reentry behaves like a focus, with centrifugal activation spanning a small part of the cycle.
Incorrect: a focus gives centrifugal activation spanning well under 90% of the cycle, with no early–late contiguity.
Correct: activation spanning ≥ 90% of the cycle, with the earliest area contiguous with the latest, indicates macro-reentry.
ep-abl-040.explication: In macro-reentry, the activation wavefront travels around a circuit that occupies almost the entire cycle: activation times span 90% or more of the cycle length, and the earliest area is contiguous with the latest, since the activation "chases its own tail". In a focal tachycardia, including localised micro-reentry, activation spreads centrifugally from a point, and the total mapped activation time is well short of the cycle length. The quality of the map (point density, annotation) must nevertheless be checked before drawing conclusions, and the diagnosis confirmed by entrainment if necessary. High-density systems (Rhythmia, multipolar catheters) make this analysis easier.
ep-abl-040.aRetenir: Activation spanning ≥ 90% of the cycle and "early meets late" = macro-reentry.
ep-abl-040.rappel: An atrial tachycardia is either focal (automaticity, triggered activity or micro-re-entry) or macro-re-entrant around an anatomical or scar-related obstacle. The target differs: for a focus, the earliest site; for macro-re-entry, a critical isthmus between two obstacles, across which a line is drawn until block is achieved. After AF ablation, the commonest macro-re-entries are perimitral, roof-dependent or cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent. Entrainment confirms that a site is part of the circuit (PPI close to the cycle length). An incomplete map or a poorly set window can mimic early meets late, so map quality comes first.

ep-abl-041.question: During AF ablation, blood pressure falls abruptly and the cardiac silhouette stops moving on fluoroscopy. What diagnosis should be considered first?
commentaires: Correct: sudden hypotension and a motionless silhouette on fluoroscopy suggest tamponade; urgent echocardiography and pericardial drainage.
Incorrect: a vasovagal reaction is a diagnosis of exclusion; it does not explain a motionless cardiac silhouette.
Incorrect: phrenic nerve palsy causes neither hypotension nor a motionless cardiac silhouette.
Incorrect: coronary air embolism can cause hypotension with inferior ST elevation, but the cardiac silhouette keeps moving.
ep-abl-041.explication: Sudden hypotension during a left atrial procedure should first suggest tamponade (perforation during transseptal puncture, catheter manipulation or an application). A motionless cardiac silhouette on fluoroscopy and echocardiography confirm the effusion. Treatment is urgent pericardial drainage, with heparin reversal by protamine as appropriate, and surgery if bleeding persists. A vasovagal reaction is a diagnosis of exclusion. Coronary air embolism can cause hypotension with inferior ST elevation, but without a motionless silhouette; phrenic nerve palsy does not cause sudden hypotension.
ep-abl-041.aRetenir: Sudden hypotension during ablation = tamponade until proven otherwise: echocardiography and drainage.
ep-abl-041.rappel: Pericardial effusion with tamponade is the most common serious acute complication of left atrial ablation. It can occur during transseptal puncture, catheter manipulation, excessive contact force or a steam pop with radiofrequency. The first signs are a fall in blood pressure, reduced motion of the cardiac silhouette and an effusion on echocardiography (transthoracic or intracardiac). Management combines subxiphoid pericardial drainage, heparin reversal where appropriate, fluid loading, and surgery if bleeding persists. Delayed tamponade, hours or days later, remains possible.

ep-abl-042.question: Three weeks after radiofrequency AF ablation, a patient presents with fever, chest pain and a transient neurological deficit. Regarding atrio-oesophageal fistula, which statements are correct?
options: It typically presents one to several weeks after the procedure
Contrast-enhanced chest CT is the investigation of choice
Upper GI endoscopy with air insufflation is recommended first line
The prognosis is very poor without urgent surgery
commentaires: Correct: the fistula typically becomes apparent one to several weeks after ablation (often 2 to 4 weeks).
Correct: contrast-enhanced chest CT is the reference diagnostic investigation.
Incorrect: air insufflation during endoscopy can cause massive air embolism; it is dangerous.
Correct: mortality is very high; only urgent surgery can improve the prognosis.
ep-abl-042.explication: Atrio-oesophageal fistula is rare but devastating. It usually presents between one and several weeks after ablation with fever, chest pain, dysphagia, neurological signs (air or septic emboli) or gastrointestinal bleeding. Contrast-enhanced chest CT is the reference diagnostic investigation. Endoscopy with air insufflation is dangerous, as it can cause massive air embolism. Treatment is urgent surgery; mortality remains very high, especially if the diagnosis is delayed.
ep-abl-042.aRetenir: Fever + neurological signs a few weeks after ablation = atrio-oesophageal fistula: CT, no endoscopy with insufflation.
ep-abl-042.rappel: The oesophagus lies against the posterior wall of the left atrium, often near the left-sided veins or the posterior wall, and its position is variable. Thermal injury (radiofrequency and, to a lesser extent, cryoablation) ranges from erythema to ulceration, which can progress to an atrio-oesophageal or oesophagopericardial fistula. Prevention relies on reducing power and duration of applications on the posterior wall, oesophageal temperature monitoring, possibly oesophageal deviation, and a proton pump inhibitor after the procedure. Pulsed field, being relatively myocardium-selective, has virtually eliminated this risk.

ep-abl-043.question: A few months after AF ablation, a patient develops progressive breathlessness, cough and haemoptysis. What diagnosis do you consider first, and how do you confirm it?
options: Right phrenic nerve palsy, on chest X-ray
Atrio-oesophageal fistula, on upper GI endoscopy
Pulmonary vein stenosis, on CT angiography
Interstitial lung disease, on chest CT
commentaires: Incorrect: phrenic nerve palsy causes breathlessness but not haemoptysis; it appears at the time of the procedure.
Incorrect: a fistula presents within a few weeks with fever and neurological signs; endoscopy with insufflation is dangerous in this setting.
Correct: delayed breathlessness, cough and haemoptysis suggest pulmonary vein stenosis; CT angiography (or MRI) with reconstruction confirms it.
Incorrect: drug-induced lung disease (amiodarone) is possible, but a delayed presentation with haemoptysis after ablation points to PV stenosis.
ep-abl-043.explication: Pulmonary vein stenosis results from lesions delivered inside the veins. It often presents late, with breathlessness, cough, haemoptysis or recurrent pneumonia in the same territory, frequently mistaken for a lung condition (infective or drug-induced pneumonitis). CT (or MRI) with pulmonary vein reconstruction confirms the diagnosis, and a perfusion scan can assess its impact. Its incidence has fallen markedly with antral isolation. Severe symptomatic cases are treated by angioplasty with or without stenting. Atrio-oesophageal fistula and phrenic nerve palsy have different presentations and timelines.
ep-abl-043.aRetenir: Breathlessness, cough, haemoptysis after AF ablation = pulmonary vein stenosis until proven otherwise.
ep-abl-043.rappel: Pulmonary vein stenosis is promoted by thermal lesions delivered inside the veins, by small-calibre veins and above all by radiofrequency; antral isolation and pulsed field have reduced its frequency. Symptoms depend on the degree of stenosis and the number of veins involved: an isolated stenosis may remain asymptomatic thanks to flow redistribution, whereas multiple severe stenoses cause segmental pulmonary venous hypertension. Diagnosis is often delayed, the condition being mistaken for lung disease. After angioplasty, with or without a stent, restenosis is common and requires imaging follow-up.

ep-abl-044.question: Phrenic nerve palsy after AF ablation most often involves:
options: The right phrenic nerve, near the right superior pulmonary vein
The left phrenic nerve, near the left inferior pulmonary vein
The left phrenic nerve, near the left superior pulmonary vein
Both phrenic nerves, near the inferior pulmonary veins
commentaires: Correct: the right phrenic nerve runs along the SVC, close to the right superior pulmonary vein; the risk is greatest with the cryoballoon.
Incorrect: the left phrenic nerve runs far from the inferior pulmonary veins; it is more at risk near the left atrial appendage.
Incorrect: the left phrenic nerve is rarely at risk during isolation of the left veins; it is the right nerve that is involved.
Incorrect: bilateral injury is exceptional, and the inferior veins are not the main site at risk.
ep-abl-044.explication: The right phrenic nerve runs along the superior vena cava and passes very close to the right superior pulmonary vein. The risk is greatest during applications to this vein, particularly with the cryoballoon; the right inferior vein is less often involved. Most palsies recover within weeks to months, especially if the application was stopped promptly. The left phrenic nerve is less often at risk (left atrial appendage, coronary sinus), and bilateral injury is exceptional. Peri-oesophageal vagal injury does occur (gastroparesis) but does not constitute phrenic nerve palsy.
ep-abl-044.aRetenir: Phrenic nerve palsy = mainly the right nerve, during applications to the right superior pulmonary vein.
ep-abl-044.rappel: Several nerves are at risk during AF ablation. The right phrenic nerve runs along the SVC and the right superior pulmonary vein; the left phrenic nerve passes over the left atrial appendage and may be affected by applications near the appendage or in the coronary sinus. With radiofrequency, the nerve is located before ablation by high-output pacing at the ablation site: diaphragmatic capture means the catheter must be moved. The periesophageal vagal plexuses can be injured during posterior wall applications, causing gastroparesis (nausea, vomiting, early satiety). Phrenic nerve palsy presents with breathlessness and an elevated hemidiaphragm.

ep-abl-045.question: Which of the following complications have been reported with pulsed field ablation?
options: Intravascular haemolysis, with a risk of acute kidney injury
More frequent pulmonary vein stenosis than with radiofrequency
A higher rate of atrio-oesophageal fistula than with radiofrequency
commentaires: Correct: haemolysis is dose-dependent and can cause acute kidney injury if many applications are delivered.
Correct: coronary spasm has been described with applications close to the arteries (mitral isthmus, cavotricuspid isthmus).
Incorrect: PFA spares the connective tissue matrix; pulmonary vein stenosis is less common than with radiofrequency.
Incorrect: thanks to its relative tissue selectivity, PFA has practically never caused atrio-oesophageal fistula.
ep-abl-045.explication: PFA registries and trials have reported dose-dependent haemolysis (especially with a large number of applications) that can cause acute kidney injury, coronary spasm with applications close to the arteries (mitral isthmus, cavotricuspid isthmus), and phrenic nerve stunning, which is usually transient. Conversely, atrio-oesophageal fistula has practically never been seen with PFA, and pulmonary vein stenosis is less common than with radiofrequency, thanks to its relative tissue selectivity. The complications common to any ablation (tamponade, vascular complications, stroke) remain. Monitoring should therefore be tailored to the energy source used.
ep-abl-045.aRetenir: PFA: watch for haemolysis, coronary spasm and phrenic stunning; the oesophageal risk is almost nil.
ep-abl-045.rappel: The complications specific to pulsed field stem from its mechanism. Electroporation of red cells releases haemoglobin; haemolysis, proportional to the number of applications, may cause haemoglobinuria (dark urine) and kidney injury, so hydration and renal monitoring are advised after a long procedure. Coronary spasm occurs with applications close to an artery and may cause ST elevation; prophylactic nitrates are often suggested. The phrenic nerve may be transiently stunned. Tissue selectivity, relative rather than absolute, conversely explains the rarity of oesophageal complications and pulmonary vein stenosis.

ep-abl-046.question: True or false: atrio-oesophageal fistula typically presents within the first 24 hours after ablation.
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is wrong; the thermal injury progresses gradually to ulceration and then fistula; symptoms appear after one to several weeks.
Correct: it is a delayed complication (often 2 to 4 weeks), which should be explained to the patient at discharge.
ep-abl-046.explication: Atrio-oesophageal fistula typically presents after a delay of one to several weeks (often 2 to 4 weeks). The thermal injury to the oesophageal wall progresses gradually to ulceration and then fistula formation. This is why patients must be told at discharge to seek urgent medical attention in the event of fever, chest pain, dysphagia or neurological symptoms in the weeks following ablation. A proton pump inhibitor is often prescribed after ablation of the posterior wall.
ep-abl-046.aRetenir: Atrio-oesophageal fistula = delayed complication (weeks), to be explained to the patient at discharge.
ep-abl-046.rappel: Complications of AF ablation follow a typical timeline. During or just after the procedure: tamponade, stroke or TIA, air embolism, phrenic nerve palsy, vascular complications. In the following days: pericarditis, delayed tamponade, haematoma, pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula at the puncture site. In the following weeks: atrio-oesophageal fistula, gastroparesis. After several months: pulmonary vein stenosis. Knowing this timeline guides the diagnosis of a post-ablation symptom and the information given to the patient at discharge, particularly on the warning signs that require urgent medical attention.

ep-abl-047.question: Which oral anticoagulation strategy is recommended around AF ablation in a patient who is already anticoagulated?
options: Stop 5 days before, with low-molecular-weight heparin bridging
Stop 48 hours before, no bridging, resume the next day
Switch to aspirin during the periprocedural period
Continue uninterrupted, or omit a single DOAC dose
commentaires: Incorrect: heparin bridging increases bleeding without reducing thromboembolic events; it is no longer recommended.
Incorrect: a 48-hour interruption exposes the patient to thromboembolic risk with no proven bleeding benefit.
Incorrect: aspirin has no role in thromboembolic prevention in AF.
Correct: oral anticoagulation (VKA or DOAC) is continued; omitting just the morning DOAC dose is an acceptable alternative.
ep-abl-047.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines and the expert consensus recommend continuing oral anticoagulation (VKA or DOAC) uninterrupted around ablation. Compared with interruption and heparin bridging, this strategy reduces thromboembolic events without increasing major bleeding. Omitting a single DOAC dose on the morning of the procedure (minimally interrupted strategy) is an acceptable alternative; a longer interruption is not justified. Heparin bridging causes bleeding and is no longer recommended. Aspirin has no place in thromboembolic prevention in AF.
ep-abl-047.aRetenir: AF ablation: uninterrupted oral anticoagulation (or minimally interrupted for DOACs).
ep-abl-047.rappel: The peri-procedural aim is never to leave the patient without thromboembolic protection, without increasing bleeding. On a VKA, the procedure is performed with the INR within the therapeutic range; on a DOAC, treatment is continued or a single dose is omitted. Intraprocedural heparin is added, titrated to the ACT. Imaging of the appendage (TOE, CT or intracardiac echocardiography) excludes thrombus according to the risk profile and the quality of prior anticoagulation. The anticoagulant is resumed the same evening or the next day, continued for at least 2 months, and then according to the risk score. Bridging with low-molecular-weight heparin is no longer used.

ep-abl-048.question: True or false: after AF ablation that is successful at 3 months, oral anticoagulation can be stopped in a patient with a CHA₂DS₂-VA score of 3, since he is in sinus rhythm.
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is wrong; long-term anticoagulation depends on CHA₂DS₂-VA, not on rhythm; with a score of 3, it must be continued.
Correct: asymptomatic recurrences are common and ablation has not been shown to reduce stroke; anticoagulation is continued.
ep-abl-048.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines recommend continuing oral anticoagulation for at least 2 months after ablation in all patients, and then deciding on long-term therapy according to the CHA₂DS₂-VA thromboembolic risk score, not according to the apparent success of the ablation. Asymptomatic recurrences are common, and ablation has not been shown to reduce stroke. A patient with a score of 3 should therefore remain anticoagulated. Left atrial appendage occlusion may be considered if anticoagulation is contraindicated, not merely because the ablation was successful.
ep-abl-048.aRetenir: After ablation, anticoagulation depends on CHA₂DS₂-VA, not on the rhythm achieved.
ep-abl-048.rappel: The 2024 ESC guidelines assess thromboembolic risk in AF with the CHA2DS2-VA score, which removes the sex criterion: heart failure, hypertension, age ≥ 75 years (2 points), diabetes, previous stroke, TIA or embolism (2 points), vascular disease, age 65–74 years. Anticoagulation is recommended from 2 points and should be considered at 1 point. The score applies regardless of the type of AF (paroxysmal, persistent, permanent), AF burden or rhythm strategy, and it is reassessed regularly. Percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion is an option reserved for patients with a contraindication to long-term anticoagulation.

ep-abl-049.question: According to the 2024 ESC guidelines, beyond what duration of AF should early cardioversion not be performed without 3 weeks of prior effective anticoagulation or a TOE?
commentaires: Incorrect: 12 hours is not the chosen threshold, even though some risk already exists between 12 and 48 hours.
Correct: the 2024 ESC guidelines lowered the threshold to 24 hours; beyond that, 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation or a TOE before cardioversion.
Incorrect: 48 hours is the former threshold, abandoned in the 2024 ESC guidelines.
Incorrect: 7 days is the historical boundary between early and delayed cardioversion, not the thromboembolic safety threshold.
ep-abl-049.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines lowered the safety threshold to 24 hours: beyond that, early cardioversion is not recommended without at least 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation or a TOE ruling out thrombus. The former 48-hour threshold was based on older data; studies have shown a non-negligible thromboembolic risk between 12 and 48 hours, especially in high-risk patients. In practice, the duration of an episode is often uncertain, which should encourage caution. Anticoagulation should be started as early as possible in patients who are candidates for cardioversion.
ep-abl-049.aRetenir: ESC 2024: AF > 24 h = 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation or a TOE before cardioversion.
ep-abl-049.rappel: The embolic risk of cardioversion stems from two phenomena: thrombus already present in the left atrial appendage, dislodged when atrial contraction resumes, and thrombus forming after cardioversion during atrial stunning. Hence two stages of prevention. Before: if AF has lasted more than 24 h or for an unknown duration, effective anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks or TOE excluding thrombus. After: anticoagulation continued for at least 4 weeks, then according to the risk score. If TOE shows thrombus, cardioversion is postponed until after prolonged anticoagulation and repeat imaging. These rules apply to both electrical and pharmacological cardioversion.

ep-abl-050.question: After cardioversion of AF, for how long at minimum must anticoagulation be continued, regardless of the risk score?
commentaires: Incorrect: post-cardioversion atrial stunning lasts far longer than 48 hours; stopping so early exposes the patient to thrombus formation.
Incorrect: one week does not cover the mechanical recovery of the atrium.
Incorrect: two weeks is still not enough; the consensus minimum is 4 weeks.
Correct: anticoagulation is continued for at least 4 weeks, then long term according to CHA₂DS₂-VA.
ep-abl-050.explication: After cardioversion, the atrium shows transient mechanical stunning: atrial contraction recovers only gradually, over several weeks, which predisposes to thrombus formation despite sinus rhythm. Anticoagulation must therefore be continued for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion, then long term according to the CHA₂DS₂-VA score. Stopping early (a few days to two weeks) is a classic error. In some very low-risk patients with AF of less than 24 hours' duration, post-cardioversion anticoagulation may be debated, but the general rule remains 4 weeks.
ep-abl-050.aRetenir: After cardioversion: anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks, then according to CHA₂DS₂-VA.
ep-abl-050.rappel: Atrial stunning follows any return to sinus rhythm, whether conversion is electrical, pharmacological or spontaneous: electrical activity is normal, but contraction of the atrium and appendage remains reduced for several weeks. Thromboembolic risk is therefore highest in the days and weeks that follow, even if a pre-cardioversion TOE was normal: TOE does not remove the need for post-cardioversion anticoagulation. The same rules apply to atrial flutter. Beyond the minimum period, whether to continue anticoagulation no longer depends on the rhythm achieved but on the thromboembolic risk score.

ep-abl-051.question: A patient with a left pectoral pacemaker requires external electrical cardioversion for AF. What is good practice?
options: Antero-apical pads, with one paddle placed over the can
Antero-posterior pads away from the can, then a device check
VOO mode programmed for one month after the shock
commentaires: Incorrect: a paddle must never be placed over the can; the current may damage the generator and the lead–myocardium interface.
Correct: antero-posterior pads at least 8 cm from the can, then device interrogation (thresholds, reset).
Incorrect: prolonged asynchronous programming is pointless; only a check before and after the shock is needed.
Incorrect: cardioversion is possible in a patient with a device, with precautions over pad placement and a device check.
ep-abl-051.explication: Cardioversion is possible in a patient with a device, with precautions: pads placed away from the can (ideally at least 8 cm), preferably in the antero-posterior position so that the current vector is perpendicular to the pacing system. The shock may cause a transient rise in pacing thresholds, a device reset or, rarely, injury to the lead–myocardium interface. The device must therefore be checked before and after the procedure and reprogrammed if necessary. A paddle must never be placed over the can. Prolonged asynchronous reprogramming is pointless.
ep-abl-051.aRetenir: Cardioversion with a device: antero-posterior pads away from the can and a device check afterwards.
ep-abl-051.rappel: An external shock can affect the device in two ways: directly at the generator, or through current channelled along the lead to the electrode–myocardium interface. Possible consequences are a transient or lasting rise in capture threshold, with a risk of loss of capture in a pacemaker-dependent patient, and a power-on reset returning the device to a backup mode. Hence pads placed at a distance and along an axis perpendicular to the lead, rhythm monitoring and device interrogation after the shock. In an ICD patient, internal cardioversion by the device itself is sometimes possible.

ep-abl-052.question: In the modernised classification of antiarrhythmic drugs (Lei et al., 2018), which class corresponds to If current (HCN channel) blockers such as ivabradine?
commentaires: Incorrect: class IV comprises calcium handling modulators, including rate-slowing calcium channel blockers.
Incorrect: class VII corresponds to "upstream" target modulators (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, omega-3 fatty acids, statins).
Correct: class 0 comprises HCN channel (If current) blockers, including ivabradine.
Incorrect: class Ic corresponds to sodium channel blockers with slow kinetics (flecainide, propafenone).
ep-abl-052.explication: The modernised Vaughan Williams classification retains classes I to IV, with subdivisions, and adds new ones. Class 0 comprises HCN channel (If current) blockers, represented by ivabradine, which slows sinus node automaticity. Class Ic corresponds to sodium channel blockers with slow kinetics (flecainide, propafenone), class IV to calcium handling modulators (including rate-slowing calcium channel blockers), and class VII to "upstream" target modulators (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, omega-3 fatty acids, statins). Classes V (mechanosensitive channels) and VI (gap junctions) have also been added.
ep-abl-052.aRetenir: Modernised Vaughan Williams: class 0 = ivabradine (If); classes V to VII are new.
ep-abl-052.rappel: The Lei et al. (2018) classification extends Vaughan Williams according to molecular target. Class 0: HCN channel blockers (If). Class I: sodium channel blockers, with Ia, Ib, Ic and a class Id for the late sodium current (ranolazine). Class II: autonomic modulators, broadened beyond beta-blockers (for example muscarinic agents and adenosine). Class III: potassium channel modulators. Class IV: calcium handling modulators, including calcium channel blockers. Classes V to VII: mechanosensitive channels, gap junctions and upstream targets related to remodelling. A single drug may belong to several classes.

ep-abl-053.question: What are the classic contraindications to flecainide?
options: Paroxysmal AF in a structurally normal heart
commentaires: Correct: the CAST trial showed excess proarrhythmic mortality with flecainide after myocardial infarction.
Correct: negative inotropy and proarrhythmia contraindicate flecainide in LV dysfunction.
Incorrect: this is its preferred indication, for pharmacological cardioversion or prevention of recurrence.
Incorrect: hypertension without significant hypertrophy or other heart disease does not contraindicate flecainide.
ep-abl-053.explication: Flecainide (class Ic) is reserved for patients without significant structural heart disease. The CAST trial showed excess mortality with flecainide and encainide in post-infarction patients, owing to a proarrhythmic effect. It is also contraindicated in LV dysfunction (negative inotropy, proarrhythmia) and in significant conduction disease not protected by a pacemaker, since it slows conduction. Hypertension without significant ventricular hypertrophy is not a contraindication, unlike marked LVH. Paroxysmal AF in a structurally normal heart is, on the contrary, its preferred indication, for pharmacological cardioversion or prevention of recurrence.
ep-abl-053.aRetenir: Flecainide: never in ischaemic heart disease or LV dysfunction (CAST).
ep-abl-053.rappel: Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) are sodium channel blockers with slow kinetics: they markedly slow conduction, and their effect increases with heart rate (use dependence), so QRS widening is more pronounced during exercise. Significant QRS widening on treatment calls for a dose reduction or discontinuation. They can unmask a Brugada pattern and worsen conduction disease. Their place is AF in a heart without significant structural disease, for pharmacological cardioversion or prevention of recurrences, always with an AV nodal blocking agent. Cardiological reassessment is needed if heart disease develops during treatment.

ep-abl-054.question: A patient is taking flecainide for paroxysmal AF. Which specific risk justifies routinely adding an AV nodal blocking agent?
options: Slow 1:1 conducted flutter with wide QRS
QT prolongation with torsades de pointes
Hyperthyroidism induced by the iodine load
commentaires: Correct: flecainide can organise AF into slow flutter (200 to 250/min) conducted 1:1 with widened QRS; the AV nodal blocking agent prevents this.
Incorrect: torsades mainly concern sotalol and class III drugs; an AV nodal blocking agent would not prevent them.
Incorrect: an AV nodal blocking agent would worsen bradycardia; this is not the risk that justifies the combination.
Incorrect: iodine-induced thyroid dysfunction is an effect of amiodarone; flecainide contains no iodine.
ep-abl-054.explication: Flecainide can organise AF into atrial flutter and slow the flutter rate (for example to around 200 to 250/min). This slower flutter can then be conducted 1:1 through the AV node, with a very fast ventricular rate and QRS complexes widened by flecainide, which may mimic VT and be poorly tolerated. This is why an AV nodal blocking agent (beta-blocker or rate-slowing calcium channel blocker) is classically added. Thyroid dysfunction due to the iodine load is an adverse effect of amiodarone. QT prolongation and torsades mainly concern sotalol and class III drugs. Bradycardia may occur, but an AV nodal blocking agent would only make it worse.
ep-abl-054.aRetenir: Flecainide: always add an AV nodal blocking agent to prevent 1:1 conducted flutter.
ep-abl-054.rappel: Each family of antiarrhythmic drugs has its own proarrhythmia. Class IA and III drugs (sotalol, dofetilide) prolong the QT interval and cause torsades de pointes. Class IC drugs slow conduction: slow atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction, monomorphic VT with very broad QRS, sometimes incessant, especially in structural heart disease. Rate-slowing agents (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) cause bradycardia and block, and digoxin toxicity various arrhythmias. Amiodarone, despite QT prolongation, carries a relatively low risk of torsades. Knowing these profiles guides monitoring: QT for class III drugs, QRS width and AV nodal blockade for class IC drugs.

ep-abl-055.question: Which are classic adverse effects of long-term amiodarone?
commentaires: Correct: being very rich in iodine, amiodarone causes hypo- or hyperthyroidism; TSH should be monitored regularly.
Correct: pulmonary fibrosis or interstitial pneumonitis is a serious effect, to be considered in the presence of breathlessness or cough.
Correct: photosensitivity and blue-grey skin discoloration are classic with long-term use.
Incorrect: hyperkalaemia is not an effect of amiodarone; it is seen rather with ACE inhibitors, ARBs or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
Incorrect: gynaecomastia is a classic effect of spironolactone or digoxin, not of amiodarone.
ep-abl-055.explication: Amiodarone, which is very rich in iodine and has a long half-life, causes many adverse effects: thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism), pulmonary fibrosis or interstitial pneumonitis, liver injury, photosensitivity and blue-grey skin discoloration, corneal microdeposits and neuropathy. Regular monitoring of TSH and liver function tests, and of lung function if symptoms occur, is required. Hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia (spironolactone, digoxin) are not among its adverse effects. It also interacts with VKAs, digoxin and some statins.
ep-abl-055.aRetenir: Amiodarone: monitor thyroid, lungs, liver, skin and eyes.
ep-abl-055.rappel: Amiodarone is a multichannel antiarrhythmic drug (class I, II, III and IV effects), highly lipophilic, with a very long half-life (several weeks), which requires a loading dose and explains both its delayed onset of action and the persistence of its effects after discontinuation. It is the antiarrhythmic drug that can be used in significant structural heart disease, particularly HFrEF, but its cumulative, dose-dependent, multi-organ toxicity makes it second-line when an alternative exists. Its interactions are important: potentiation of VKAs (INR monitoring), increased digoxin levels, and interaction with some statins. Baseline tests and scheduled monitoring are required throughout treatment.

ep-abl-056.question: Regarding dronedarone, which statements are correct?
options: It is contraindicated in unstable or NYHA III–IV heart failure (ANDROMEDA)
It is contraindicated in permanent AF (PALLAS)
It can cause a modest rise in creatinine by inhibiting its tubular secretion
It is the antiarrhythmic drug of choice in severe heart failure with reduced EF
commentaires: Correct: ANDROMEDA showed excess mortality in recently decompensated severe heart failure; contraindicated in unstable or NYHA III–IV HF.
Correct: PALLAS showed an excess of cardiovascular events in permanent AF.
Correct: it inhibits the tubular secretion of creatinine, which rises modestly without any real fall in filtration.
Incorrect: it is contraindicated in severe HF; amiodarone remains the antiarrhythmic drug that can be used in HFrEF.
ep-abl-056.explication: The ANDROMEDA trial was stopped because of excess mortality with dronedarone in patients with recently decompensated severe heart failure, hence the contraindication in unstable or NYHA III–IV HF. PALLAS showed an increase in cardiovascular events in permanent AF, in which it is contraindicated. In ATHENA, in paroxysmal or persistent AF, it reduced cardiovascular hospitalisation or death. It raises creatinine modestly by inhibiting its tubular secretion, without truly impairing filtration, which must be interpreted accordingly. In severe HFrEF, amiodarone remains the antiarrhythmic drug that can be used.
ep-abl-056.aRetenir: Dronedarone: never in severe/unstable HF or in permanent AF.
ep-abl-056.rappel: The choice of a rhythm-control antiarrhythmic drug in AF depends first on the underlying heart disease. Without significant structural heart disease: flecainide or propafenone (with an AV nodal blocking agent), or dronedarone. In ischaemic or valvular heart disease, HFpEF or stable HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction: dronedarone, or amiodarone. In HFrEF: amiodarone. Class IC sodium channel blockers are excluded whenever there is ischaemic heart disease or LV dysfunction. Safety comes before efficacy; amiodarone, the most effective, is reserved for situations with no alternative because of its extracardiac toxicity.

ep-abl-057.question: Which precaution is essential when starting sotalol?
options: Check TSH monthly for the first six months
Monitor liver function tests and lung function
None: it is used like any other beta-blocker
Monitor QT, potassium and renal function
commentaires: Incorrect: thyroid monitoring applies to amiodarone, not sotalol.
Incorrect: liver and lung monitoring apply to amiodarone.
Incorrect: its class III effect prolongs the QT in a dose-dependent manner; it is not a simple beta-blocker.
Correct: initiation with ECG monitoring of the QT, dose adjusted to renal clearance, and potassium and magnesium corrected.
ep-abl-057.explication: Sotalol combines beta-blocking activity (class II) with a class III effect (blockade of the IKr potassium current) that prolongs the QT in a dose-dependent manner: it is therefore not a beta-blocker like any other. The risk of torsades de pointes is increased by renal impairment (renal elimination), bradycardia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and female sex. It is therefore started with ECG monitoring of the QT, at a dose adjusted to creatinine clearance. Combining it with a potassium-wasting diuretic is dangerous. Thyroid, liver and lung monitoring apply to amiodarone.
ep-abl-057.aRetenir: Sotalol: monitor QT, potassium and renal function; risk of torsades.
ep-abl-057.rappel: The risk of torsades de pointes on a QT-prolonging drug results from an accumulation of factors: female sex, bradycardia or pauses, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, renal impairment for renally cleared drugs, co-prescription of other QT-prolonging drugs (some macrolides, antipsychotics, antiemetics), and pre-existing long QT. Monitoring relies on measuring the QTc before and after initiation or any dose change; excessive prolongation requires dose reduction or discontinuation. Torsades typically occur after a short–long–short sequence, hence the danger of pauses.

ep-abl-058.question: In an ICD patient, which antiarrhythmic drug tends to lower the defibrillation threshold?
commentaires: Incorrect: class Ib sodium channel blockers (lidocaine, mexiletine) tend to raise the defibrillation threshold.
Correct: class III potassium channel blockers such as sotalol (which is also a beta-blocker) tend to lower the defibrillation threshold.
Incorrect: according to some data, flecainide tends rather to raise the defibrillation threshold.
Incorrect: long-term amiodarone may modestly raise the threshold, usually without consequence with current devices.
ep-abl-058.explication: Antiarrhythmic drugs that mainly block potassium currents (class III such as sotalol, which is also a beta-blocker, or dofetilide) tend to lower the defibrillation threshold. Beta-blockers may also lower it slightly. Conversely, class Ib sodium channel blockers (lidocaine, mexiletine) tend to raise it, as does flecainide according to some data; propafenone has little effect. Long-term amiodarone may modestly raise the defibrillation threshold, although this is not usually significant with current devices. After starting or increasing an antiarrhythmic drug in an ICD patient, programming should therefore be reviewed (detection zones, as the VT rate may be slowed) and, if necessary, the safety margin checked.
ep-abl-058.aRetenir: Sotalol lowers the defibrillation threshold; amiodarone, lidocaine and mexiletine tend to raise it.
ep-abl-058.rappel: The defibrillation threshold is the minimum energy that reliably terminates VF; the ICD must deliver a shock with an adequate safety margin above this threshold. Broadly, potassium channel blockers, which prolong the refractory period, tend to lower it, whereas sodium channel blockers tend to raise it. Antiarrhythmic drugs also interact with the ICD in other ways: slowing VT below the programmed detection rate (VT undetected or untreated), altered ATP efficacy, raised pacing thresholds and proarrhythmia. Any change in antiarrhythmic therapy justifies a review of the programming.

ep-abl-059.question: True or false: class Ic antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) can raise pacing thresholds, which justifies a pacemaker check after they are started in a patient with a device.
commentaires: Correct: by slowing conduction and reducing excitability, class Ic drugs can raise capture thresholds; these should be rechecked.
Incorrect: the statement is true; threshold rises on class Ic drugs are documented, especially at high doses or with hyperkalaemia; a check is prudent.
ep-abl-059.explication: Class Ic sodium channel blockers slow conduction and reduce myocardial excitability, which can raise capture thresholds, especially at high doses or with concomitant hyperkalaemia. In a pacemaker-dependent patient, loss of capture can have serious consequences. It is therefore prudent to check thresholds after starting the drug or increasing the dose, and to keep an adequate safety margin (or to use automatic capture management algorithms). In ICD patients, flecainide can also raise the defibrillation threshold (propafenone appears to have little effect on this threshold).
ep-abl-059.aRetenir: Class Ic drug started in a patient with a device: recheck pacing thresholds.
ep-abl-059.rappel: The capture threshold varies with the state of the myocardium in contact with the electrode. It rises with hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypoxia, ischaemia or acute infarction, certain drugs (mainly class IC antiarrhythmic drugs) and during maturation of the interface after implantation; corticosteroids tend to lower it. The programmed safety margin must cover these variations: typically an amplitude of about twice the threshold. Automatic capture management algorithms adjust the output to the measured threshold. Any change in these factors in a pacemaker-dependent patient should prompt a capture check.

ep-abl-060.question: What is the "pill-in-the-pocket" strategy with flecainide, and what are its conditions?
ep-abl-060.reponseAttendue: A single oral dose of flecainide self-administered by the patient at the onset of an AF episode (200 mg if < 70 kg, 300 mg if ≥ 70 kg), combined with an AV nodal blocking agent, in a patient without structural heart disease who has infrequent episodes, after a first dose has been tested under monitoring in hospital.
ep-abl-060.explication: This strategy allows pharmacological cardioversion outside hospital, avoiding emergency department visits. It is reserved for patients without ischaemic heart disease or LV dysfunction, without significant conduction disease, and with infrequent, well-tolerated episodes. The first dose must be taken under monitoring to confirm efficacy and the absence of proarrhythmia or post-conversion bradycardia. A beta-blocker or rate-slowing calcium channel blocker is added to limit the risk of 1:1 conducted flutter. The patient should seek medical attention if the episode persists or is poorly tolerated.
ep-abl-060.aRetenir: Pill-in-the-pocket: single dose of flecainide 200–300 mg, structurally normal heart, first dose tested under monitoring.
ep-abl-060.rappel: Pharmacological cardioversion of recent-onset AF depends on the patient's cardiac profile. Without significant structural heart disease: flecainide or propafenone, effective within a few hours, or vernakalant, rapid but contraindicated in particular with hypotension, recent acute coronary syndrome, severe heart failure or severe aortic stenosis. With structural heart disease: amiodarone, safer but slower to act. The rules of thromboembolic prevention are the same as for electrical cardioversion. The single-dose outpatient strategy requires a selected, educated patient in whom tolerance has been checked.

ep-abl-061.question: True or false: sotalol has both beta-blocking (class II) and class III properties.
commentaires: Correct: the l-isomer carries the beta-blocking activity, and both isomers block IKr (class III), hence bradycardia and QT prolongation.
Incorrect: the statement is true; sotalol is not a pure beta-blocker; its class III effect explains the risk of torsades.
ep-abl-061.explication: Sotalol is a racemic mixture: the l-isomer carries most of the beta-blocking activity, while both isomers block the IKr potassium current (class III effect), prolonging repolarisation and the QT interval. It therefore combines bradycardia and QT prolongation, two factors that promote torsades de pointes. For this reason its use in AF is now more restricted and requires close monitoring. Amiodarone also has multiple properties (classes I, II, III and IV).
ep-abl-061.aRetenir: Sotalol = beta-blocker + class III, hence the risk of torsades.
ep-abl-061.rappel: Sotalol is excreted unchanged by the kidneys, without hepatic metabolism: its dose depends on creatinine clearance, and it accumulates in renal impairment. The beta-blocking effect predominates at low doses, the class III effect increasing with dose. Like other IKr blockers, it shows reverse use dependence: prolongation of repolarisation is more marked at slow heart rates, so the risk is greatest during bradycardia and pauses. This combination explains its limited role in AF, with strict selection criteria and QT monitoring.

ep-abl-062.question: Which drug is one of the first-line rate-control agents for the ventricular rate in AF?
commentaires: Incorrect: mexiletine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic drug used for ventricular arrhythmias.
Incorrect: ivabradine acts on the sinus node, not the AV node; it does not slow the ventricular response in AF.
Correct: beta-blockers such as bisoprolol slow AV nodal conduction; they are first-line rate-control agents.
Incorrect: flecainide controls rhythm, not rate; used alone, it can even accelerate the ventricular response.
ep-abl-062.explication: According to the 2024 ESC AF guidelines, first-line rate control relies on beta-blockers (bisoprolol, metoprolol, etc.), rate-slowing calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, reserved for patients with LVEF > 40%) or digoxin, depending on the patient's profile. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines advise against verapamil and diltiazem in all HFrEF, now defined as LVEF < 50%, and place beta-blockers first line in this setting. These drugs slow conduction through the AV node. Flecainide is a rhythm-control antiarrhythmic drug, not a rate-control agent, and can even accelerate the ventricular response if used alone. Mexiletine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic drug used for ventricular arrhythmias. Ivabradine acts on the sinus node, not the AV node.
ep-abl-062.aRetenir: Rate control in AF: beta-blocker, rate-slowing calcium channel blocker (to be avoided in LV dysfunction) or digoxin; class I antiarrhythmic drugs are not rate-control agents.
ep-abl-062.rappel: Rate control in AF initially aims for a lenient target (resting heart rate below 110 bpm), tightened if symptoms persist. Rate-control drugs all act on the AV node: beta-blockers, usable whatever the LVEF; rate-limiting calcium channel blockers, avoided in LV dysfunction because of their negative inotropic effect; and digoxin, useful in combination or with hypotension but not very effective on exertion. Combinations are common, with monitoring for bradycardia. Amiodarone is only a fallback in the acute setting or after failure. Rhythm-control antiarrhythmic drugs are not rate-control agents, and ivabradine acts only on the sinus node.

ep-abl-063.question: According to the 2024 ESC guidelines, in which situation may percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion be considered?
options: Patient preference, as a first-line alternative
Paroxysmal AF with a CHA₂DS₂-VA score of 0
commentaires: Correct: the 2024 ESC guidelines allow it to be considered (class IIb) in patients with a contraindication to long-term anticoagulation.
Incorrect: in a patient who can take an anticoagulant, occlusion does not replace it as first-line therapy.
Incorrect: with a score of 0, no thromboembolic prevention is indicated.
Incorrect: successful ablation justifies neither appendage occlusion nor stopping anticoagulation.
ep-abl-063.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines state that percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion may be considered (class IIb) in patients with AF who have a contraindication to long-term oral anticoagulation, to prevent ischaemic stroke. It does not replace first-line anticoagulation in a patient who can take it. A score of 0 does not justify any thromboembolic prevention. Surgical appendage occlusion, as an adjunct to anticoagulation, is recommended in patients undergoing cardiac surgery (LAAOS III), which is a different situation.
ep-abl-063.aRetenir: Percutaneous appendage occlusion: for patients who cannot take long-term anticoagulation.
ep-abl-063.rappel: In non-valvular AF, the vast majority of left atrial thrombi form in the appendage, hence the idea of excluding it mechanically. Percutaneous occlusion is performed via a femoral venous and transseptal approach, with a device implanted at the appendage ostium; it carries its own complications (pericardial effusion, device embolisation, device-related thrombus, residual leak). Transient antithrombotic therapy remains necessary after implantation, while endothelialisation takes place. In a patient who can take an anticoagulant, anticoagulation remains the reference; occlusion is an alternative for those who cannot take it long term.

ep-abl-064.question: What are the two main things to look for on follow-up imaging (TOE or CT) a few weeks after percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion?
ep-abl-064.reponseAttendue: 1) Device-related thrombus, which requires antithrombotic therapy to be resumed or intensified. 2) Peri-device (residual) leak, assessing its size (a large leak, classically > 5 mm, is considered significant). The position and stability of the device and the absence of effusion are also checked.
ep-abl-064.explication: After appendage occlusion, follow-up imaging is usually performed between 6 weeks and 3 months. Device-related thrombus is associated with an increased risk of stroke and requires the antithrombotic regimen to be adjusted. Peri-device leaks are common; large leaks are associated with an excess of thromboembolic events. Antithrombotic therapy after implantation depends on the device and on bleeding risk (for example, short-term anticoagulation, or dual antiplatelet therapy followed by aspirin alone). The result of this imaging guides simplification of the regimen.
ep-abl-064.aRetenir: After appendage occlusion: look for device-related thrombus and significant peri-device leak.
ep-abl-064.rappel: Percutaneous appendage occlusion is planned with imaging (TOE or CT) to analyse the appendage morphology, measure its ostium to choose the device size and exclude thrombus. During implantation, position, stability, device compression and seal are checked before release. After the procedure, the device is gradually endothelialised; until this coverage is complete, its surface may be thrombogenic. Antithrombotic therapy is therefore stepped down, and its simplification depends on follow-up imaging. Device-related thrombus or a significant leak changes treatment and follow-up.

ep-abl-065.question: True or false: the LAAOS III trial showed that surgical left atrial appendage occlusion, performed during cardiac surgery in patients with AF, allows oral anticoagulation to be stopped without increasing the risk of stroke.
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is wrong; in LAAOS III most patients remained anticoagulated; occlusion reduced stroke as an adjunct, not as a replacement.
Correct: surgical occlusion reduces ischaemic stroke (4.8% vs 7.0%) on top of anticoagulation, which it does not replace.
ep-abl-065.explication: The statement is false. LAAOS III randomised 4811 patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication to surgical left atrial appendage occlusion or no occlusion. After a mean follow-up of 3.8 years, occlusion reduced the risk of ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism (4.8% vs 7.0%), while most patients remained on anticoagulation. The trial therefore did not evaluate stopping anticoagulation: occlusion is an adjunct, not a substitute. The 2024 ESC guidelines recommend this surgical occlusion in patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery, with anticoagulation continued according to the risk score.
ep-abl-065.aRetenir: LAAOS III: surgical appendage occlusion in addition to (not instead of) anticoagulation = fewer strokes.
ep-abl-065.rappel: Surgical left atrial appendage occlusion is performed during cardiac surgery, by excision, suturing or clip placement; its efficacy depends on complete occlusion, since a residual stump or incomplete closure may remain a source of emboli. In a patient with AF undergoing cardiac surgery for another reason, it is recommended by the 2024 ESC guidelines as an adjunct to anticoagulation, which remains guided by the risk score. Three situations should be distinguished: concomitant surgical occlusion (adjunct to anticoagulation), percutaneous occlusion (alternative when anticoagulation is contraindicated), and surgical AF ablation, which targets the rhythm.

ep-abl-066.question: Immediately after AV junction ablation, at what lower rate is the pacemaker classically programmed for the first few weeks?
commentaires: Incorrect: a low rate from the outset promotes QT prolongation and torsades after junction ablation.
Incorrect: 60 to 70 bpm is still insufficient during the first few weeks; the risk of torsades persists.
Correct: 80 to 90 bpm for the first few weeks (often 1 to 2 months), followed by gradual reduction, prevents torsades.
Incorrect: such a high permanent rate would be excessive and harmful.
ep-abl-066.explication: Early sudden deaths have been reported after AV junction ablation, attributed to repolarisation abnormalities (QT prolongation) promoted by the abrupt bradycardia and the change in activation sequence, with a risk of torsades de pointes. To limit this risk, the lower rate is programmed at 80 to 90 bpm for the first few weeks (often 1 to 2 months), then gradually reduced. A low rate (40 to 70 bpm) from the outset is therefore not advisable. A rate of 110 to 120 bpm would be excessive and harmful. Rate response is usually activated afterwards.
ep-abl-066.aRetenir: After AV junction ablation: lower rate 80–90 bpm initially to prevent torsades.
ep-abl-066.rappel: Ventricular repolarisation adapts to heart rate, but with a delay. After AV junction ablation, the abrupt change from fast AF to a fixed paced rate, combined with a new ventricular activation sequence, can prolong the QT interval and expose the patient to torsades de pointes during the adaptation period. Hence a lower rate initially set high, then reduced in steps. As the patient is pacemaker-dependent, system reliability is essential: stable leads, checked thresholds and adequate safety margins. This is also why implantation often precedes ablation by a few weeks.

ep-abl-067.question: Which pacing mode and type of pacing should be favoured in a patient with permanent AF and reduced LVEF who is a candidate for AV junction ablation (ablate and pace)?
ep-abl-067.reponseAttendue: A ventricular mode without atrial sensing (VVIR; an atrial lead serves no purpose in permanent AF), with physiological pacing that avoids the dyssynchrony of pure RV pacing: biventricular resynchronisation (CRT) or conduction system pacing (preferably left bundle branch area, or His bundle with a backup lead), depending on local expertise.
ep-abl-067.explication: After AV junction ablation, the patient becomes 100% pacemaker-dependent. Pure RV pacing causes ventricular dyssynchrony that can worsen LV function, especially if it is already impaired. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend CRT rather than RV pacing in patients with reduced LVEF who are candidates for AV junction ablation. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines recommend considering AV junction ablation combined with CRT (class IIa, level B1) in highly symptomatic, poorly controlled permanent AF with at least one HF hospitalisation. The 2025 ESC consensus on conduction system pacing considers it a reasonable option in this indication regardless of LVEF, with a preference for LBBAP (or His bundle pacing with a backup ventricular lead). In permanent AF, an atrial lead is of no use; the mode is VVIR (or the biventricular equivalent). It is often advised to implant the device before the ablation to confirm lead stability.
ep-abl-067.aRetenir: Ablate and pace with reduced LVEF: CRT or conduction system pacing (LBBAP preferred), in VVIR mode.
ep-abl-067.rappel: Conduction system pacing captures the native conduction tissue to achieve rapid, synchronous ventricular activation, unlike myocardial RV pacing. His bundle pacing produces the most physiological activation, but its thresholds are higher and less stable, so a backup lead is used in pacemaker-dependent patients. Left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) offers lower and more stable thresholds. When AV junction ablation is planned, the ablation site must stay away from the His lead so as not to compromise capture. In permanent AF, an atrial lead is unnecessary; biventricular CRT is the strategy tested in the randomised APAF-CRT trial.

ep-abl-068.question: In an elderly patient with highly symptomatic permanent AF and a persistently fast rate despite maximum tolerated rate-control therapy, which non-pharmacological rate-control strategy can be offered?
options: Slow pathway modification to slow AV conduction
Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation, then resumption of rate-control drugs
Pacemaker implantation alone, with no ablation
AV junction ablation after pacemaker implantation
commentaires: Incorrect: AV nodal modification has been abandoned because its effect is unpredictable (AV block or inadequately controlled rate).
Incorrect: the cavotricuspid isthmus is the target for typical flutter; this line does not control the rate in AF.
Incorrect: a pacemaker alone protects against bradycardia but does not slow the fast ventricular response of AF.
Correct: ablate and pace: pacemaker implanted (often a few weeks earlier), then AV junction ablation; anticoagulation maintained.
ep-abl-068.explication: The tracing shows AF with a fast ventricular response. When pharmacological rate control fails or is not tolerated, and a rhythm control strategy is not desirable, AV junction ablation combined with pacemaker implantation (ablate and pace) provides perfect, regular rate control; the device is often implanted a few weeks before the ablation to confirm lead stability. The 2024 ESC guidelines recommend considering it in these patients. The patient becomes pacemaker-dependent, and anticoagulation must be continued according to the risk score, since AF persists. Isthmus ablation treats flutter, a pacemaker alone does not slow fast AF, and slow pathway "modification", being unpredictable, has been abandoned.
ep-abl-068.aRetenir: Permanent AF refractory to rate control: AV junction ablation + pacing, with anticoagulation maintained.
ep-abl-068.rappel: In AF, rate-control strategy follows a stepwise escalation. It starts with a rate-control drug suited to the patient's profile, then drug classes are combined (for example a beta-blocker with digoxin) if the target is not reached. If this fails, the value of rhythm control is reconsidered. When neither pharmacological rate control nor rhythm control is feasible or desirable, ablate and pace offers definitive control, at the cost of irreversible pacemaker dependence; it is therefore mainly offered to older patients in permanent AF. The choice of pacing modality depends on the LVEF and the heart failure context.
ep-abl-068.legende: Permanent AF despite a beta-blocker and digoxin

ep-abl-069.question: How is the left atrium usually accessed for AF ablation?
options: Femoral artery, then retrograde aortic route
commentaires: Incorrect: the retrograde aortic route leads to the left ventricle; it does not allow practical work in the left atrium.
Correct: the catheters are advanced via the inferior vena cava, then puncture of the fossa ovalis gives access to the left atrium.
Incorrect: the coronary sinus is used as a landmark and for recording, not for access to the left atrium.
Incorrect: the epicardial approach is reserved for some VT ablations.
ep-abl-069.explication: AF ablation is performed via femoral venous access: the catheters are advanced through the inferior vena cava to the right atrium, then transseptal puncture (at the fossa ovalis) gives access to the left atrium. This puncture is often guided by echocardiography (intracardiac or transoesophageal) and fluoroscopy. The retrograde aortic arterial approach leads to the left ventricle and does not allow practical work in the left atrium. The coronary sinus, cannulated via the femoral or subclavian route, serves as a landmark and for recording. The epicardial approach is reserved for some VT ablations.
ep-abl-069.aRetenir: AF ablation: femoral venous access + transseptal puncture.
ep-abl-069.rappel: Transseptal puncture crosses the fossa ovalis, the thinnest part of the interatrial septum, with a needle (mechanical or radiofrequency) advanced in a long sheath from the superior vena cava and then withdrawn towards the fossa. Guidance combines fluoroscopy and, increasingly, intracardiac or transoesophageal echocardiography, which shows tenting and directs the puncture site. The main risks are aortic puncture, perforation of the atrial wall and tamponade. A patent foramen ovale may allow direct crossing. The iatrogenic atrial septal defect usually closes spontaneously.

ep-abl-070.question: What is the main benefit of a 3D electroanatomical mapping system during ablation?
options: Combining 3D anatomy, electrical signals and catheter position
Delivering and titrating ablation energy at the tissue interface
Continuously measuring LVEF and intracardiac pressures
Eliminating all use of fluoroscopy during the procedure
commentaires: Correct: the map reconstructs the chambers, projects activation and voltage onto them and localises the catheter in real time, with less fluoroscopy.
Incorrect: the energy comes from a separate generator; the mapping system does not deliver it.
Incorrect: electroanatomical mapping measures neither ventricular function nor pressures.
Incorrect: it greatly reduces fluoroscopy but does not always eliminate it (transseptal puncture, positioning).
ep-abl-070.explication: 3D mapping systems (CARTO, EnSite, Rhythmia) reconstruct a virtual anatomy of the chambers and project electrical information onto it: local activation times, voltage, fractionation. They localise the catheter in real time, which makes it possible to tag ablation points, return precisely to a site and greatly reduce X-ray exposure, although not always eliminate it. They do not deliver the energy, which comes from a separate generator, and do not measure ventricular function. They are particularly useful for complex circuits (atypical flutters, scar-related VT).
ep-abl-070.aRetenir: 3D mapping = anatomy + electrical data + catheter localisation, with less fluoroscopy.
ep-abl-070.rappel: Different types of map answer different questions. The activation map (local activation time) locates a focus or follows a re-entrant circuit; the propagation map animates the activation wavefront. The voltage map delineates scar and low-voltage areas, which are useful for substrate ablation. Tags mark sites of interest: abnormal potentials, entrainment sites, His, phrenic nerve. High-density multipolar catheters speed up the acquisition of thousands of points. Merging with CT, MRI or intracardiac echocardiography refines the anatomy. Reliability depends on signal annotation and point density.

ep-abl-071.question: What is the most common, though usually benign, complication of an ablation procedure via femoral access?
options: Complete AV block requiring a pacemaker
commentaires: Incorrect: tamponade is serious but less common (around 1% in AF ablation).
Incorrect: AV block mainly concerns ablation close to the conduction system (slow pathway, septal pathways) and remains rare.
Incorrect: pulmonary vein stenosis has become rare with antral isolation.
Correct: haematoma, false aneurysm or arteriovenous fistula are the most common complications; ultrasound-guided puncture reduces them.
ep-abl-071.explication: Femoral access-site complications (haematoma, false aneurysm, arteriovenous fistula) are the most common complications of ablation, promoted by anticoagulation and the number of sheaths. Ultrasound-guided puncture has reduced them markedly. Tamponade, at around 1% in AF ablation, is less common but serious. Atrio-oesophageal fistula and pulmonary vein stenosis are rare but serious. AV block mainly concerns ablation close to the conduction system (slow pathway, septal pathways). Access-site monitoring is part of post-procedural nursing care.
ep-abl-071.aRetenir: Most common complication of ablation: the access site; ultrasound-guided puncture reduces it.
ep-abl-071.rappel: Femoral access, venous for most ablations and arterial for the retroaortic approach or pressure monitoring, exposes the patient to several local complications: haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula and, more rarely, retroperitoneal haematoma. The latter, favoured by a puncture that is too high (above the inguinal ligament), presents with hypotension or flank pain without visible haematoma and requires urgent imaging. Predisposing factors are anticoagulation, the number and size of sheaths and inadvertent arterial puncture. Ultrasound guidance, careful haemostasis and monitoring of the puncture site limit their frequency.

ep-abl-072.question: A young woman has recurrent episodes of this tachycardia, with abrupt onset and offset. The EP study confirms typical AVNRT. What is the treatment of choice to prevent recurrence?
commentaires: Incorrect: a pacemaker has no role; AVNRT is not a bradycardia.
Incorrect: the cavotricuspid isthmus is the target for typical flutter, not AVNRT.
Incorrect: long-term amiodarone is not justified in a young patient, given its toxicity.
Correct: slow pathway ablation cures more than 95% of AVNRT, with a risk of AV block below 1% (class I).
ep-abl-072.explication: The tracing shows a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at around 180/min with no visible P wave, typical of AVNRT (retrograde P wave hidden within the QRS). For recurrent symptomatic AVNRT, slow pathway ablation has a class I recommendation in the 2019 ESC guidelines: it is curative in more than 95% of cases, with a risk of AV block below 1%. Long-term amiodarone is not justified in a young patient, given its adverse effects. A pacemaker has no role, and the cavotricuspid isthmus relates to flutter.
ep-abl-072.aRetenir: Recurrent symptomatic AVNRT: slow pathway ablation, the curative treatment of choice.
ep-abl-072.rappel: In a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia, the position of the retrograde P wave points to the mechanism. In typical AVNRT, atria and ventricles are activated almost simultaneously: the P wave is hidden in the QRS or visible at its end (pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-S in the inferior leads). In orthodromic AVRT, the retrograde P wave is later, in the ST segment, because the impulse must cross the ventricle before returning up the accessory pathway. A P wave preceding the QRS (long RP) suggests atrial tachycardia, atypical AVNRT or AVRT using a slowly conducting decremental pathway. Acutely, vagal manoeuvres then adenosine, whose effect is also diagnostically useful.
ep-abl-072.legende: Episode of palpitations recorded in the emergency department

ep-abl-073.question: True or false: after AV junction ablation for permanent AF, oral anticoagulation can be stopped since the ventricular rate is controlled.
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is wrong; junction ablation only controls the ventricular response; the atria remain in AF and the embolic risk persists.
Correct: AF persists, and anticoagulation continues according to CHA₂DS₂-VA.
ep-abl-073.explication: AV junction ablation controls only the ventricular response: the atria remain in AF and the thromboembolic risk is unchanged. Anticoagulation must therefore be continued according to the CHA₂DS₂-VA score. This is a common misconception among patients, who feel much better and believe they are "cured" of their AF. It should also be remembered that these patients become pacemaker-dependent, which has implications for follow-up and programming.
ep-abl-073.aRetenir: Ablate and pace: AF persists, and so does anticoagulation.
ep-abl-073.rappel: After AV junction ablation, two facts coexist: the atria remain in AF, and the ventricles depend entirely on the pacemaker. The first requires anticoagulation to be continued according to the risk score, as in any AF. The second changes device management: close follow-up or remote monitoring, vigilance about battery depletion and lead integrity, adequate capture safety margins, programming an asynchronous mode when interference is expected (diathermy) and planning generator replacement ahead of time. Any loss of capture exposes the patient to asystole.
